subtopic: ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
subsubtopic: NATIONAL CONFERENCE ON WOMEN AND THE CONSTITUTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Yesterday I raised a question in the House concerning statements made by Doris Anderson, president of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, which accused the minister responsible for the status of women of interfering unduly in the workings of the council by exerting pressure on the executive of the council to cancel its national conference on the constitution because it might be embarrassing to the government.
In light of the unsatisfactory answer I received, the necessity to maintain the independent nature of this council and the need for a national conference of women on the constitution, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday):
That this House demands that the minister refrain from exerting any further pressure or taking punitive action against this independent advisory council, and that we as responsible parliamentarians endorse the plans of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, originally undertaken last summer, to hold a national conference of women on the constitution now scheduled for February 13 and 14.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion concerning an increasingly urgent matter in several areas of Canada.
In view of the fact that VIA Rail trains have experienced undue delays during the Christmas holidays; that there was a shortage of locomotive fuel; that the CN gave priority to freight trains, thus delaying passenger trains in eastern Canada which were already more than 30 hours late; that emergency teams were not on duty to clear the tracks in eastern Quebec, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais):
That the House direct the Canadian Transport Commission to launch an investigation into the numerous delays and derailments that occurred between December 15, 1980, and January 12, 1981; that the commissioners recommend remedial measures to be taken during the rush period; and that the report be submitted to the House before June 1, 1981.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare by her silence has recently allowed steps to be taken which would commercialize the buying, selling and processing of human blood for profit by a federal Crown corporation, and whereas this action contravenes the voluntary spirit of the Red Cross blood donor program and can only serve to escalate the costs of health care even further, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That this House hereby instructs the CDC owned Connaught Laboratories Limited that the gift of life, that is to say human blood, is not a commodity of commercial traffic, nor is it to be processed into plasma for financial gain; and further, that this House pledges its unreserved support to the Canadian Red Cross in its desire to establish an in-house facility for the processing of human blood into plasma.

Madam Speaker, it is seldom that I rise on a question of privilege. This is only the second time I have done so in the eight years I have been a member of Parliament, so you will understand the seriousness I attach to the question of privilege I address to you today.
Yesterday the minister responsible for the status of women was charged by the president of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women with manipulation of the council's plans when he used his ministerial office to exert pressure on the council's executive to cancel an upcoming conference on the constitution.
The Advisory Council on the Status of Women was established in 1973 to provide independent, objective advice "to the government and to the public on matters of interest and concern to women and to advise the government on actions that the council deems necessary to improve the position of women in society". The council was carrying out that mandate when it made plans last summer to hold a national conference on the constitution to deal with a broad range of women's issues in various constitutional jurisdictions.
That conference, which was originally slated for last September, had to be rescheduled for February of this year. The conference plans were already well advanced and have only been called into question following a meeting last Friday between members of the executive committee of the council and the minister. It was at that meeting, the president now charges, that the minister exerted pressure to have the council change its plans to hold a constitutional conference for fear of possible embarrassment to the government.
The council's terms of reference, as spelled out by the then minister responsible for the status of women, the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), on May 31, 1973, as reported at page 4282 of Hansard, ensured that the council would report to Parliament as well as to the minister responsible by making its recommendations and its reports public. In this way it was assumed that the advice and recommendations proffered would be both independent and objective.
In this respect the council is comparable to other councils which offer independent advice to government. 1 refer to councils such as the Economic Council of Canada and the International Joint Commission. I know of no occasion when a member of Parliament has felt it necessary to raise a question of privilege based on government interference with the work of these two bodies or, indeed, of any other council, commission or consultative body which offers independent advice to government and Parliament.
It is my contention that in interfering with the plans presented to the government "on actions that the council deems necessary to improve the position of women", in this case the

holding of a constitutional conference on women's issues, the minister interferes not only with the council but also with the privilege of members of Parliament to receive and to question the government concerning that advice, as promised in the statement by the then minister responsible for the status of women on May 31, 1973.
I mentioned that the Advisory Council on the Status of Women is comparable to the Economic Council of Canada or the International Joint Commission in the way it proffers advice to government, but it is clear that it is not comparable in that it is the only such body whose recommendations are interfered with by the minister responsible, and whose members are manipulated. The Advisory Council on the Status of Women is subjected to different and, I would say, discriminatory treatment, which is a further affront to members of Parliament and to the privilege of members of Parliament, particularly women members of Parliament.
In reply to questions put by me yesterday concerning the accusation made by the president of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women that the minister and the government were attempting to influence the council into cancelling its proposed constitutional conference, something which I am sure the minister knows the executive committee on its own cannot do, the minister replied that the president's statements were "not accurate or proper". In other words, he refuted her charge. Since then the president has reiterated her stand with charges of manipulation and with the statement that, and I quote:
Mr. Axworthy's attempt at influencing the council marks the first time the government has interfered with the independent government-appointed organization.
We have two entirely contradictory views of what happened in that meeting of last Friday when members of the executive of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women met with the minister. We have the statements of the president of the council and those of the minister. Parliamentary rules dictate that I must accept the word of the minister with respect to his non-interference in this matter, except for his suggestion of regional conferences, but I feel that he is being less than honest with the House in detailing the role he played in this matter, that he has misled the House, and that indeed there is a possibility he may have deliberately misled the House, given the initial and subsequent statements by the president of the council.
This is no mere tempest in a teapot. It is a very serious matter when the president of an extremely prestigious council feels it may be necessary to tender her resignation because of recent manipulation of their organization by a federal cabinet minister. I feel it is a serious question of privilege and of my rights as a member of Parliament that there should be two such contradictory positions on this matter and that we, as parliamentarians, do not have sufficient information on what transpired at the meeting held last Friday with the minister to determine what type of influence the minister exerted. Those of us who are interested in maintaining the integrity and
independence of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women should have the right to be more adequately informed on the nature of the pressure which the minister has been charged with exerting on the council.
If you find, Madam Speaker, that I have a question of privilege in this matter, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the matter of the statements made in the House on January 12, 1981, by the minister responsible for the status of women respecting directions given by him to the executive of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, and the significant discrepancy between the minister's assertions and those of the president of the council, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too treat the statement made by the hon. member with a great deal of seriousness. I only wish that she would follow her own advice, that is, to make some effort to obtain the proper facts and information before she makes the kinds of charges she has just been guilty of suggesting. She has asked for third party confirmation as to who is right.
If I might, I should like to read into the record of the House a statement which was issued by the executive committee of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women just today. It states:
The executive committee of the CACSW is appalled by the action of its president, Doris Anderson.
The executive committee in December expressed concern about the timing of the constitutional conference.
Because of the successful presentation before the joint committee and the distribution of research papers on the constitution to the women of Canada, the issue of the entrenchment of rights had been properly and thoroughly dealt with by the advisory council.
Sensing that the timing of the planned February conference was no longer opportune, and feeling strongly that the conference ought to be rescheduled, the executive committee of the advisory council sought a meeting with Mr. Axworthy-
I underline "sought a meeting".
-to discuss the matter with them.
Mr. Axworthy agreed that the issues might get a better airing at a later date but stated that the decision was the council's to make and added "we can live with it either way''.
"It was clear, after speaking with the minister" said Win Gardner, senior vice-president, "that the issues we wanted to discuss at the conference, such as jurisdiction over divorce and social services, would not be on the government's plate at that time and that therefore attention would be greatly diverted from these important issues".
"At no time was cancellation of the conference even considered", said Win Gardner. "The matter of rescheduling is to be brought before the full council meeting next week, and the executive committee will of course abide by its decision".
Author?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
That was a statement which was issued by members of the executive committee. The hon. member asked for confirmation. I suggest that unless she is prepared to say that the other members of the executive committee are not telling the truth, she will simply have to say that her statement and her allegations are wrong. I would ask her to withdraw the
January 13, 1981

statement from the records of the House because it really is unfounded.
I should like to state further that so far as I am concerned, this is primarily a matter between Mrs. Anderson and the members of the council and the executive committee. Mrs. Anderson had her own desires or ambitions overturned by the executive committee. She obviously felt compelled to take some fairly extreme action to deal with them. It is a matter which should be resolved by that council and by the executive committee.
I should point out to members of the House that on the matter of the constitutional conference, if I am guilty of interference, it was I who suggested originally to the advisory council that the conference be held. It was my suggestion and recommendation that the conference be established. The conference was cancelled by that council on the decision of its president and executive committee last fall. They decided to reschedule it. I believe they had a meeting amongst themselves earlier on to discuss the timing. They came to me as the minister to ask for my opinion and advice, and I gave it to them. I said to them that whatever choice they made, it was up to them. At no time was pressure applied, or manipulation. Those are words used by Mrs. Anderson for her own reasons. I would not attempt to manipulate that council which is an independent body. I respect its opinions, and we as the government respected them when the council made its representation on the constitution and the charter of rights, and we have responded to it.
I would simply say to you, Madam Speaker, and to members of the House, that for the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) to take the one-sided opinion of one person and to make the kinds of charges she has made without any further investigation, without making any effort to see if there was another side to the case, is really an abrogation of my privileges. I would go to the extent of saying that she resorted to grandstanding-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: I would not say this is a laughing matter. I do not think it is a matter which should be used for partisan reasons. What is really at stake is the integrity of that council, and that is a question which should be decided by that council and should not be brought into the forum of partisan politics as the hon. member has done.

Madam Speaker, it comes right down to this: do we accept what the minister said yesterday that the statement of Mrs. Anderson, the president of the council, is inaccurate, or do we accept the minister's assurance to us that he does not make any attempt to interfere with or manipulate the council, particularly the executive committee of that council? If I am asked which I accept, there is no doubt in my mind that I accept what Mrs. Anderson has said because she is the person who has credibility in this country. She is the person, despite being a Liberal appointment, who has had the guts to stand up
Privilege-Miss MacDonald
to the government and to stand up to the minister over the past several months.
On three occasions the minister publicly stated, once in Montreal, once in Saskatoon, and the third time elsewhere, that he was not happy or satisfied with what the council was doing in its work on the constitutional proposals. He said it was getting "bad legal advice". He did everything possible to undermine the work of that council in preparing its work for the constitutional committee of the House and Senate on the constitutional proposals of his own government. His whole record in the last several months is one of undermining the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, and particularly its president. He would dearly love her to resign. He wants to get someone in there as he has some of the vice-presidents there now who are total patsies-
Oh, oh!

That is what he wants. I shall name one in particular because I named her when she was appointed to the council. She was moved out of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) office, put into the council as a mole-
Oh, oh!
-to keep an eye on the president of the council. She was there to make sure-
Hear, hear!

Everyone knows this, if the minister does not. No one wanted her on the council, not a single member. She was put on it because the Liberals wanted to have a mole there whom they could trust to do their bidding-
Oh, oh!
The minister knows who I am talking about, as does everyone in the House.
Who?
An otherwise very agreeable person, except in this connection, and her name is Hellie Wilson, and we all know that.
Shame!

The minister is apparently denying the statement made by Mrs. Anderson and repeated in The Globe and Mail today. He says she is inaccurate. That is why this matter should go before a committee of the House to get to the truth of it.
1 have also other evidence which I will be glad to bring before the committee to investigate its accuracy, namely, that when she was away for a day last week, as I think she said- this was after the minister had agreed to the conference being held and had booked a room for it; do not forget, Madam Speaker, the minister had already arranged for a room to be booked for this mid-February conference and he did that back

January 13, 1981
Privilege-Miss MacDonald
in December, he agreed to be their luncheon speaker-all this was done.
One day last week when the president of the council was away, the mole took it upon herself as acting president, as reported in The Globe and Mail today, to meet:
-Mr. Axworthy and later reported to Mrs. Anderson that the minister preferred that the conference be cancelled.
Miss Wilson also called back press releases sent out earlier in the day to announce the conference dates.
Those press releases were all prepared before Mrs. Anderson left town, and they were to have been sent out. It continues:
All releases were intercepted except those that arrived at the offices of The Globe and Mail and a television network. These were picked up later in the day by a messenger.
That was done at the minister's bidding; that was done by an acting president for a day of that council. The other members of the executive committee were talked into supporting it because they too are loyal Liberal supporters of the minister, and one from his own city who is particularly loyal-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am having some difficulty here because I am afraid the hon. member is stating things which should be followed by real charges.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has made a statement, and the hon. member should not doubt the statement of the minister.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: She could disagree with it, but she could not put it in doubt. I am just asking the hon. member if she could choose her words more carefully because I am wanting to get up nearly every minute to tell her that she is going beyond what is parliamentary. I will now ask her to proceed.

Madam Speaker, I do not want to be unparliamentary. 1 am, as is the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), really very upset by this interference with an independent council. If this were to happen with the Economic Council of Canada, every member of this House would be up proclaiming and protesting about it. But I shall do my very best to wind up by keeping within the guidelines Your Honour suggested to me.
I shall wind up by saying that the advisory council must be an independent advisory body. That is what it is designed to be and to do. What has given most of the women of this country joy in the last year and a half has been the fact that the president of that council was independent; it has given every woman in this country joy. As the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien) said, it has made possible a first-rate presentation to the constitutional committee, probably one of the best given to that
committee. It has made possible all kinds of research that the previous chairman or president of that council never undertook. It has had all kinds of influence for the good of the women of Canada.
Since this must never be repeated, this political interference, I would ask that the motion of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, which I would have gladly seconded, should be accepted by Madam Speaker so that the matter can be thoroughly cleared up and never repeated.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will be brief in my intervention on this matter. I must say that I find it quite remarkable that a minister of the Crown should stand and conduct himself in such a way as we have just witnessed in relation to a public servant who reports to that minister and, to the best of our knowledge, still apparently holds his trust, not having been dismissed from her position by the minister. I cannot recall a situation in which there has been similar treatment of a public servant by a minister of the Crown here on the floor of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But what I want to pick up on is the suggestion of the minister that what is at issue here is simply a question- if I am quoting him correctly, and 1 believe I am-between Mrs. Anderson and the council. That is not at all what is at issue here. The issue is the relation and the conflict between an agency which was established to bring issues to the attention of the public of Canada and of the Parliament of Canada, and whether or not that agency has been allowed the unfettered ability to carry out its mandate, to carry out its responsibilities, to speak and act as it is authorized to speak and act, without intrusions by a minister of the Crown, without the kind of manipulation which has been alleged by the president of the council.
Today the minister brought in a statement allegedly prepared by the executive committee of the council. Apparently he has not discussed the matter with the president. I presume, had he discussed the matter with the president, it would have been courteous for him to have so indicated-he now indicates that he has done that. I am surprised that he did not indicate it at that time and did not indicate to us what action would flow from the discussion between himself and the president. As the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has indicated, the point is that when this matter arose we had two conflicting versions as to what had occurred in relation to a recommendation made by a public body and actions taken by a public body, part of whose purpose is to bring before the government and before the public certain matters relating to public policy and to women in Canada.
Now we have a third matter before the House of Commons raised by the intervention of the hon. member for New West-minster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett). The hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam has now added new allegations of
January 13, 1981

fresh manipulation by the minister in the activities of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women.
It has been argued that we must accept the word of the minister on this matter. Parliament is in the dilemma that it must also accept the word of the president of the advisory council. Now we are in the further dilemma that we must also accept the word of the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam whose statements on these matters are at least as credible and as deserving of being accepted by members of the House of Commons as the statements of the minister of the Crown.
First of all, there is a very real question as to whether an agency which can function effectively only if it is independent has had that independence interfered with by the minister. Also there is the very real question that we have before the House of Commons a conflict in the recording of the role of the minister by the minister and by certain members of the advisory council on the one hand, and by the still serving president of the advisory council on the other hand. Finally, we have a conflict between the testimony of the minister who is a member of this House, whose word we are supposed to accept, and a member of the House of Commons, the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam, who, by the rules of the House, made statements we are bound to accept.
In the circumstances, and having regard to the precedent which can flow and to the damage which can be done to every independent agency that is to bring matters before the public of Canada-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-having regard to the dangers which can flow if that kind of manipulation occurs and if that kind of manipulation is allowed to continue, I would suggest that the privileges of members of the House of Commons are very seriously affected by the allegations which have been made here. The best way to resolve the question would be to refer it to a committee.
I recall that earlier, when the minister had questions raised on which he felt some confidence, he volunteered they be referred to the appropriate committee. Now he stands in the way of a similar reference. If he is absolutely confident of the position which he stated on the floor of the House, then I believe it would be wise for him to do now what he did earlier when the propriety of his conduct was called into question, and have the matter referred to the appropriate committee.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must say that on its face I do not feel there is a question of privilege. It seems to me, on its face, that we have a difference of opinion as to what took place and what actions or what implications flowed from what took place. But the interventions on this particular question were made very seriously, and charges were quite serious. I do want to look into it, and I will rule on it at a later date.

subsubtopic: TOKYO ROUND-TARIFF REDUCTIONS
speechtext: Did the Department of (a) Industry, Trade and Commerce (b) Agriculture (c) Finance (d) Energy, Mines and Resources (e) Employment and Immigration (f) Regional Economic Expansion (g) Fisheries and Oceans (h) Labour prepare regional impact studies on the effect of the Tokyo Round of tariff reductions, as embodied in the June 2, 1980, Ways and Means motion and, if so, what is the title of each study?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TOKYO ROUND-TARIFF REDUCTIONS
speechtext:
I am informed by the following departments as follows:
(a)	Industry, Trade and Commerce:
Industry, Trade and Commerce, in co-operation with other departments, participated in a continuing evaluation of Canadian interest in the MTN, both from a sectoral and regional point of view. Although the publication of the results did not specifically identify regional impacts, this can be derived in large measure through an appreciation of the relative importance of various sectors of the Canadian economy to the particular regions of Canada.
(b)	Agriculture Canada:
No. However, departmental staff worked with the interdepartmental negotiating team to prepare information on the agricultural impact included in the press package released.
(c)	Finance Canada:
Consideration of the regional impact of the tariff reductions agreed to in the multilateral trade negotiations (MTN) was an integral part of the government's on-going decision-making process. One of the Canadian objectives in the MTN was to achieve a mix of gains in foreign markets and concessions in Canadian tariff and non-tariff barriers which would represent a reasonable result from the point of view of the different Canadian
provinces and regions. In order to assist in identifying regional interests the government consulted closely with provincial governments throughout the MTN. Consultations took place, for example, through the Canadian Trade and Tariffs Committee and the office of the Canadian co-ordinator for the MTN as well as by means of a federal-provincial conference on the MTN.
(d)	Energy, Mines and Resources Canada:
No.
(e)	Employment and Immigration Canada:
No.
(f)	Regional Economic Expansion:
DREE did not prepare a regional impact study of the effects of the Tokyo Round of tariff reductions. However, information concerning possible sectoral impacts was used in combination with other factors in a study which was focused on the larger issue of industrial adjustment.
(g)	Fisheries and Oceans:
No.
(h)	Labour Canada:
No.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council) moved:
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE TIME ALLOCATION FOR SECOND READING OF BILL C-48
speechtext:
That, in relation to Bill C-48, an act to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, one sitting day shall be allotted to the further consideration of second reading stage of the bill; and that at 15 minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business on that day, any proceedings before the House shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of second reading stage of the bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I move this motion following the notice I gave last night. 1 had the opportunity last evening to expose briefly the reasons why the government had to take this position at this time. I, as the government House leader, would have liked to see that bill referred to the standing committee on energy before the Christmas break. Even if there was no such agreement, we were expecting this bill to be referred to the committee before December 19, hoping that the committee would have had an opportunity to hear witnesses and look at the bill, at the same time hoping that the House of Commons would be able to deal with some of the other business that must be dealt with on an urgent basis. But such reference was not made and we had to face the reality that now, it being January 13, we still have this bill on the floor for second reading. In fact, today is the fifth day of debate on the second reading stage of this bill.
Yesterday, when 1 spoke to my colleagues on the other side, 1 still thought and hoped that we could come to an agreement on a reasonable length of time required to dispose of second reading of this bill. 1 suppose my hopes were too high. 1 could not obtain that agreement, which is why we are forced today to move the motion about which I am speaking.
There are four reasons why I feel this motion is well founded under the circumstances. Essentially what we are discussing in Bill C-48 is only a part, although an important part, of our
January 13, 1981

national energy policy. Yesterday, when the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was speaking she said at the beginning of her remarks that in her mind she was speaking not only on a single bill but on a part, an important part, of the government's national policy on energy. I said that 1 agreed with that view. But if we follow that view we must admit that many days so far have been used by members on both sides to discuss the energy policy of the government, including Bill C-48.
The energy policy of the government was outlined clearly when the budget speech was read, and six days of debate followed the budget speech when most members spoke on energy. Then there were two special debates of three days each on the proclamation to put into effect some parts of the Petroleum Administration Act. Altogether this required six days of the time of the House of Commons. So, if we look at the six days which were used during the debate on the budget, plus the six days that were used in the debate on the proclamation, which I just mentioned, we are up to 12 days, when members on both sides had an opportunity to speak on energy. Then we brought in Bill C-48, which is one element of the energy policy, and so far four days have been taken up speaking on the second reading stage of this bill. Mr. Speaker, that is the first reason why I think we are justified at this stage in asking the House to limit debate on the second reading stage of Bill C-48.
The first reason of the four I am talking about is that this is only a part, an important part, of our national energy policy. In fact we are not bringing an end to the debate, we are allocating one additional day, and the bill will be studied at length at the committee stage and then will be reported to be studied at the report stage and at the third reading stage.
The second reason why I think it is important for us to move this motion today, as I just explained in my first reason, is that so far 12 days, plus the four days on second reading, which total 16 days altogether, have been devoted almost entirely to speeches related in some way to the national energy policy of the government.
The other reason why it is time to refer this bill to committee is a very realistic reason. If we consider that we already have on the order paper some 40 items of business to deal with, and if we take into consideration the fact that the government has the responsibility to deal with the economy, energy and constitutional matters, there is absolutely no way that a reasonable government can afford to allot more than four, five or six days at a maximum on one particular stage of a bill. I sincerely feel that if we did not interfere at this stage, assume our responsibility and exercise leadership in ordering the business of the House, we would be failing the confidence which was bestowed upon us by the population of the country.
It is very easy for me to stand up and argue that this motion has been introduced to maintain the respect of Parliament and our responsibility to Canadians. If there is no agreement to the length of discussion on one stage of a particular bill, then we must exercise leadership and impose a limit on the time for
S.O.	75 c
discussion of the second reading stage so that the bill may be sent to committee and so that the House may be in a position to deal with other urgent business such as the 40 items on the order paper which I have mentioned.
Among those 40 items are other bills which relate to energy, and members on both sides will have further opportunities to make their views known with regard to the energy policy. There are also bills relating to the constitution and to the economy. It is only as a result of the attitude of the opposition parties that we are following this procedure. I cannot blame any individual members who have spoken on energy. I wish to be realistic, and I am sure hon. members will admit that so far there have been many opportunities to speak on this issue and that there will be many more opportunities over the next weeks and months both in the House and in committee. No member will be in a position to complain that the government was not reasonable and did not allow him or her to express his or her views on such an important matter.
If hon. members will be honest with themselves, what we are discussing is a limitation of time on a single stage of a single bill which represents only part of the total energy policy which has been discussed for more than 16 days now and which will be discussed at length over the next weeks and months.
Standing Order 75 with its three parts, A, B and C, is available to the government under such circumstances. Politically, it may not be very good for members of the opposition to agree to a time limit on the discussion of the stages of a bill. Perhaps they are even relieved that I have taken this direction. I have no reservations in doing so because I believe my action is in the interest of the people of Canada. Hon. members have had many opportunities to express their views, and I respect the fact that these opportunities should be available. In spite of the fact that we have imposed Standing Order 75C, hon. members will still have an opportunity to make their views known in committee.
Yesterday an hon. member of the opposition presumably received the approval of his leader to ask of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) during question period when hon. members would be able to hear witnesses on the government's energy policy. The minister's reply was to the effect that we should send the bill to committee so that witnesses could be heard. What we are attempting to do by this motion today is to put some order into the working of this place and assume our responsibility. If in the future we do not obtain agreement to reasonable time limits on the discussion of a particular bill, then it will be impossible for this House to function and we will be forced to use Standing Order 75c more frequently than has been the case in the past.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE TIME ALLOCATION FOR SECOND READING OF BILL C-48
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, quite apart from that naked threat to begin the parliamentary term 1981, I cannot recall a procedural argument which would rival in its absurdity the defence which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) has uttered for imposing closure. Just to recap it, Mr. Speaker, his argument is that if a general subject matter has been discussed frequently in this House of Commons, then that is justification for the

January 13, 1981
S.O.	75c
Government of Canada to stop and to limit arbitrarily the discussion of the details of a specific bill brought before this House. Surely that is absolutely absurd and absolutely unacceptable, not only to this Parliament but to any member on this side, and it should be unacceptable to any member on that side of the House who believes in democracy, if there are any who believe so.
What we are seeing here is the development of a very clear pattern on energy policy, and it is the same pattern which is being applied to constitutional policy. The government misleads Canadians as to the purposes of its proposals and then, just as soon as the parliamentary debate begins to reveal the real motives and the real results of government policy, Parliament is cut off.

That is what happened in the case of the constitution. The government said it wanted to put an end to British influence in Canadian constitutional matters when, in fact, the Liberal party wanted the British to settle questions which the Canadians themselves should decide. When the debate revealed the truth about its proposals, the government imposed closure in a futile effort to hide the truth from the Canadian people. And now, the Liberal government is trying once again to use the same trick in the case of energy.

On the first day of the parliamentary session the Liberal government announced that it would use its majority to stop parliamentary debate in an attempt to conceal from Canadians the damage this energy policy will do to the country. That is not only a contempt of Parliament, it shows contempt for the people of Canada and for the basic interest of this nation, and it is a betrayal of any concept of democracy. Instead of seeking the consent of the people in an open, honest way, this Liberal government tries to hide the facts from Canadians.
Let us look at this bill which Parliament will not be allowed to debate, Bill C-48. It gives the minister private powers which are perhaps the most extensive arbitrary powers ever granted a minister in this country outside wartime. Clause 12 allows the minister, alone, to decide which friend he would like to award with an exploration agreement, without calling for any other proposals. By clause 44 and clause 45, the minister, alone, may order a company to drill an oil well, whether or not that drilling makes sense. By clause 55 the minister, alone, may decide that a company is not behaving in the way that the minister would like it to behave. The minister may then, as a result of this bill which Parliament will not be allowed to debate, take away that company's permit and cancel its holdings. That is an invitation for abuse. It invites political patronage, arbitrary decision-making, and blackmail of an industry by a minister or by officials who want to force that industry to act against its own interests and to act in a way that might conform with some computer model that some economist with no understanding of the real world has dreamed up.
There are some 86 detailed clauses in this bill, a bill on which we have had less than 12 hours' discussion. Thirty-two
of the 86 clauses of this bill give the minister or the government power that is excessive and power that Parliament cannot control. It is no wonder the government does not want Canadians to know the details of the bill. It is no wonder this Liberal government cuts off debate on a bill with such provisions. Given the nature of this extraordinary ministerial power, this motion today means double closure because Parliament today is being forbidden to debate what Parliament tomorrow will be forbidden to review.
What this does is take public policy-policy decisions which should be a right of this Parliament and of the public of Canada to review, and gives them to the minister. It gives him the power to act alone, the power to practise patronage, the power to practise blackmail, the power to intrude deeply in the industrial activities of the nation and lets him do it without any parliamentary accountability, without any parliamentary scrutiny and without any parliamentary review. That is the kind of proposal that this minister and this government want the Parliament of Canada to accept, with the most severely limited debate. That, sir, is absolutely unacceptable to anyone who believes in parliamentary democracy.
1 point out to the House and to any others who are concerned about the balance between the public and the private sector, who are concerned about the aspirations of this government, that a situation which gives that kind of excessive power to one minister-to Marc Lalonde, of all people-a bill which gives that kind of arbitrary power to Marc Lalonde may focus today on the energy industry but, sir, it will lead to other industries later, at other times in the life of this country, and of the life of this government which is determined to use and abuse its powers regardless of the dangers to the country. That speaks of the private powers which the government does not want to advertise at all.
Let me deal now with the pretended purpose of this bill, which is government advertising that I believe to be false. The government pretends that its energy policy has as its purpose the increase of Canadian ownership. Instead, this policy is forcing Canadian companies to leave Canada, and therefore, this policy which Parliament is denied the right to debate is damaging Canadian ownership, is not helping Canadian ownership.

The government claims its energy program will promote the development of Canada. In fact, its program is driving jobs and investments out of Canada. For instance, this year Canadian Hunter will be spending in the States from $50 million to $100 million it had intended to invest in Canada; Home Oil has now stated that its main priority will now be to spend up to $1 billion on the purchase of an American energy company; Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas has cut back its exploration budget here in Canada by $220 million; and Union Oil has slashed by half the $70 million it had planned to spend in Canada. This means that Canadians from coast to coast will
January 13, 1981

be losing their jobs. The mere fact that drilling rigs are moving out of Canada could mean 55,000 fewer jobs here in Canada. Yet, it is impossible to discuss the matter here in the House of Commons of Canada.

The government pretends that its program will make Canada secure in energy. Its program does the opposite and that is why ministers do not want to discuss it in this country. Their program makes Saudi Arabia secure, it makes Mexico secure, it makes Venezuela secure, it makes Texas secure, but it exposes to the ravages and uncertainties of the world. Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brusnwick and the province of Quebec. Those five provinces are dependent today for part of their oil on foreign sources.
If the government continues on its way and continues to push through without parliamentary debate the kinds of measures that are in this bill, then the province of Ontario will soon be depending on foreign oil, that cannot be counted on, to heat its homes and fuel and its industries.
We have here, Mr. Speaker, a deeply dangerous bill, an immensely complicated bill and one that involves confiscation by the Government of Canada. It is a bill that involves deep intrusion into the affairs of the private sector of Canada. It is a bill that is already driving small Canadian companies to take their savings, their jobs, their expertise and to leave this country. It is a bill that hands to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that extraordinary power to interfere in the decisions made by investors across this country. It is a bill that demands debate in this House. If there has ever been a bill which required this Parliament to consider it, it is one which extends, to the extent that this does, the discretionary power sought by the government. Instead of allowing Parliament to debate this matter, however, this Government of Canada is gagging the House of Commons and is trying to stop the people of Canada from understanding what is at stake in this deeply damaging energy policy.

subsubtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE TIME ALLOCATION FOR SECOND READING OF BILL C-48
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE TIME ALLOCATION FOR SECOND READING OF BILL C-48
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are opposed to the motion that has been presented by the government House leader because, in our view, this is not the way to run the Parliament of Canada. Whatever may be the views of the various parties or the various members of this House on Bill C-48, it is an extremely important one and it deserves adequate discussion.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) seems to be concerned that we spent as much time as we have already this session on the subject of energy. He must know, as all members of the House know, that this is one of the most serious issues facing Canada-indeed, facing the world-in this decade. If time has to be spent on the subject of energy and all its aspects, then I suggest that is quite appropriate.
I recognize the impatience that the government House leader feels about debate that goes on and on. I recognize his sense of frustration when he cannot get agreement from the
S.O.	75 c
two opposition parties to shorten debate. I should like him to know, however, that there are times on this side of the House when we are tired of some of the things we hear from the other side. We are getting awfully tired of the way in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stands up, day after day, and tells us there is no real economic crisis in the country, that anything that is wrong is due to external forces, and that members of the opposition are wasting the time of the House in raising these issues.
There is nothing we can do about that, Mr. Speaker, but keep on raising the issues and keep on talking. I suggest, however, that for the government House leader to be in the position that because he is tired of hearing a debate on a certain bill, therefore it should come to an end, is not the way to run the Parliament of Canada.
I know that there are those who argue-and no doubt we will hear that argument in the debate today and probably see it in editorials, if the press comments on this day's debate- that there is a case for organizing and ordering our debate in this House of Commons instead of just letting it go on and on in some capricious way. I quite agree, but I suggest that when we have a rule that permits an unlimited second reading debate and when a debate starts that way, it is, in effect, changing the rules in the middle of the game for the government to make use of Standing Order 75c.
The government supporters would probably say that the rule is there to be used. I would remind government supporters that rules 75a, b and c were brought in back in 1969 after very extensive debate only by the use of the 1913 closure rule. Rules 75a, B and C do not represent the consensus of those who were in the House of Commons at the time those rules were passed, and they certainly do not represent the consensus of Parliament today.
I would also point out that every time any closure rule is used, either 75c or the old 1913 rule, it does damage to the atmosphere and the spirit of Parliament.
I use this opportunity once again to say that I believe we have to find a better way. The better way that I have in mind is one that I have proposed quite a few times, but I am going to take the opportunity to suggest it again today.
I believe that instead of this haphazard, ad hoc, capricious way of the government stepping in to stop a debate, the continuance of which it does not like, we should have a set up under which, at the start of the session, the government is required to give to Parliament the titles of all the bills it proposes to introduce. I think we should have the wisdom and maturity to agree that for most of those bills a time limit on second reading would be in order-say a time limit of two days.
There are two categories of bills on either side of that main body that I think we have to consider. There are some bills that are so routine, so housekeeping in nature, that they hardly need any time on the floor of the House at all. They could be referred without debate to committees.

January 13, 1981

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
At the other end of the spectrum there are serious and controversial bills to which the application of closure of any kind, I believe, is wrong. I say, as a spokesman for one of the opposition parties, that we would be prepared at the beginning of a session to agree to a time limit on a great body of bills at second reading if, at the same time, we were given the right to say we will give you these five or six bills and send them to committee without any debate because they are routine and housekeeping in nature, on the understanding that in return for the five or six that we are prepared not to debate at all, there will be another five or six crucial bills which the opposition chooses, and on which there would be no curtailment of time at all.
When I have made this proposal on previous occasions the question has arisen: what about bills which the government might not know about at the start of a session but might bring in later on? 1 say those bills have to be in a category that the opposition can debate them as it wishes. Oppositions are not always unreasonable. A while ago we had an urgent request for a bill having to do with the environment. The case was made to us that it was important. We had only heard of it for a few days and we put it through in a very short space of time.
The business of what we do with bills that come in late is something we can handle in a responsible way. But I press again my idea that we plan the whole session. We know what the rules are, and those rules having been agreed upon and laid down, should be followed. As I say, I am prepared to go for a general limitation on most bills provided that we have the right to trade off five, six or eight bills without debate, in return for five, six or eight bills of our choosing that we insist should be debated without time limit. I think something like that could be done with estimates as well.
At any rate, what I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, is that those of us who are opposing this motion are not persons with a negative approach who want to stop everything and block Parliament all the time, but we have ideas as well as to how this place should be made to work. 1 think that along the lines I have suggested, or along similar lines, a better way could be found than this business of the government House leader stepping in when he gets tired of a debate and is frustrated because he cannot get the opposition parties to agree, and so changes the rules in the middle of the game.
This is an important bill in a very important field, Mr. Speaker. It is an issue which will concern us greatly throughout the 1980s in Canada and around the world. I think it is pretty shortsighted and unfair to Parliament for the government to bring in this motion at this time.
When the two hours of this debate are over, Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party will be voting against this closure motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: S O. 75C
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate. First, I welcome the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)
who, unlike the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), has made constructive suggestions to the House which I think should be looked at by all House leaders later in the session. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre obviously made these comments in good faith. He recognizes an argument can be made that the opposition does perhaps tend to prolong debate unnecessarily as an argument can also be made that government acts too hastily.
The government is not acting hastily at this particular point in time. The member for Winnipeg North Centre talks about the frustration of the government House leader (Mr. Pinard). It is not a question of frustration, it is a question of getting the government's program through Parliament. That is what Canadians want.
Since we have come back after the last election, we have heard criticism, week in and week out, from the opposition that it wants action on the economy, on energy, and on the constitution. After a reasonable period of debate and second reading of this bill, which I emphasize is only one aspect of the government's energy program, the opposition criticizes us for moving the debate along and putting it before the rest of the members in committee.
It is quite appropriate that we move it at this time. We have a number of other matters coming before the House. We have the constitution, and other budget and energy bills. There has been this discussion of parliamentary reform. But 1 ask both the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the member for Winnipeg North Centre how they expect us to deal with parliamentary reform if we are bogged down with lengthy debates on every single piece of legislation which comes through?
I want to draw to the attention of hon. members of the House the whole question of second reading debate. It is my understanding that second reading debate exists to establish whether one is for or against a principle involved in a particular piece of legislation.
In the United Kingdom, second reading is dealt with in a much more efficient manner than it is here. In fact once the motion is put, debate continues until all speakers have exhausted their arguments, and then comes the final question. I believe this procedure was suggested for the Canadian House of Commons about 13 years ago. The Special Committee on Procedure which sat during 1967 to 1968 recommended that second reading motion be debated until the question was put, that is, it could go on all night until all arguments were exhausted, as it is done in Westminster. However, this suggestion was rejected by members of the House at the time. Nevertheless, I hope we can take a serious look at this proposal. It has had all-party support.
A distinguished former member for Halifax-East Hants, who was deputy speaker at one time and is now an eminent member of the bench in Nova Scotia, Mr. Robert McCleave, commented along the same lines, and his remarks can be found in Hansard at pages 905 and 907 for March 16, 1972.
January 13, 1981

I welcome the spirit in which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made his interjection. 1 would hope we could look at the whole aspect of parliamentary reform, including second reading debate, later on in this session.
As I said before, the opposition argues for decisive action on the part of the government. In fact the NDP is so exercised about matters that it is declaring a state of emergency for the economy. Yet, when we try to proceed and try to make more time to debate other economic matters-

subsubtopic: S O. 75C
speechtext:
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: S O. 75C
speechtext:
I am talking about the multinational oil companies. Yes, they have contributed much to this country, but they have done very well by the riches of this country. But when the Government of Canada comes along and says, "Look, the situation is such that you are making perhaps exorbitant profits or benefiting too much from the situation at hand", then we receive all kinds of objections from the oil industry.
It is quite apparent that the oil industry is using them very effectively-and I say using because it comes through in arguments made by the official opposition. Members of the official opposition, I think, are somewhat misguided in their views on this particular subject. It makes me sad that members of this House would be so blind as not to see that they are defending a narrow, privileged group which is being asked to share fairly in the economic wealth and growth of this country.
We are not talking about confiscation. We are talking about sharing and fairness. It has been an accepted principle in Canada, Great Britain and the United States over the past 50 or 60 years that you pay according to your ability to pay. That is all we are asking of the oil industry in this case. Indeed, that is all we are asking of the producing provinces, that those which have wealth are expected to pay taxes. If an individual sees his income grow, he expects to pay taxes accordingly. We are saying that one taxes wealth where it exists.
I have no compunction in agreeing with and supporting strongly the arguments made by the President of the Privy Council in bringing forward this time allocation motion. It is not closure. The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) in his booming voice talked about closure. It is not closure. The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton-and I quoted this when we discussed this matter last June-said on December 7, 1979, as reported at page 2149 of Hansard:
I have only done this because there is no end in sight to the debate, none whatsoever.

most ill-conceived energy policies in the history of this country will not be the multinational oil companies. They can take care of themselves. They are the strong ones, they are the big ones.

The rigs are now going south because of the uncertainties and some certainties created by this national energy policy.
I speak now as a member for Ontario. This is the most wilfully wrong approach to development this country has ever seen. The government has sown the wind and it will reap the whirlwind. The country will be divided as a result of what the government has done. Instead of being able to marshal all the resources, federal and provincial, to achieve self-sufficiency on the one hand and fighting the economic problems on the other, we have developed, augmented, and increased the sense of regionalism in this country. That is wrong.
There is nothing wrong with Canadianizing the oil industry. However, it is wrong for the government to cast such uncertainty on the business community that ordinary Canadians who work in it will suffer from that uncertainty. That is what is wrong and that is why I say the parliamentary secretary is so absolutely wrong. If he believes what he said is true, he is misguided. I feel I have to tell him that.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) said we had debated for too long. He implied that the opposition held up this debate. When this debate ended last night, ten members of the official opposition, my party, had spoken, and ten members from the government party had spoken, the same number. Who is holding up the debate, if indeed it is being held up? Three members from the New Democratic Party had spoken. Who is holding up the debate?
At ten o'clock last night we had exhausted about 12 hours of debate. By our traditions, that is not very long in the parliamentary sense. Including yesterday, the last day in which we debated the merits of the substance, we had used four parliamentary days.
The case which the government House leader made with respect to delay, frustration, his efforts and those of others, has been absolutely destroyed by the statistics related to this debate. He went on to say that we had six days of budget debate. That is true. However, a budget debate can range over
a whole host of subjects, not just energy. Indeed, that is precisely what happened in the budget debate. It was not an energy debate, as he said. We had six days on the proclamation. There is no case today for closure or allocation of time. The only difference between allocation of time and closure is that when we debate allocation of time they have to give us at least one day. They do not have to do that with respect to closure. A rose by any other name is still a rose in my book. They are both distasteful. One is merely less distasteful than the other.
What concerns me more, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre touched on it, is the statement made by the minister at the end of his speech. He served notice on this House of Commons today and threatened the members of this House that if we do not do what he wants, if we do not kowtow to the cabinet, or if we dare to continue to debate matters of importance, he by himself is going to cut us off. Because our relationship with him is good on a personal level, that relationship, which ought to exist, ought not to be foreclosed in advance with respect to subsequent pieces of legislation.
This House operates well if attitudes are good and sound. The atmosphere in this House has been soured by allocation of time on the borrowing bill and closure on the constitutional matters. Now there is allocation of time with respect to this bill after a very short debate. This matter is of fundamental importance to members of Parliament from every part of this country.
One of the problems of this whole system and what may lead to these debates is the fact that there is no opportunity under our existing rules for private members of Parliament to deal with the things which are important to them and to their constituents. Our committee structure is a shambles. Ministers do not have to answer questions. If they move from one portfolio to another, they cannot be asked questions on their former portfolios. The question period is inadequate. I suggest it would be well for the government House leader not to turn his mind to foreclosing in advance long debates, as he did today.
Today the government House leader issued a naked threat. Rather, he should turn his attention to how the raw power of government, and majority government in particular, can be balanced in some way by the ability of this House to hold government accountable for its actions. That ability is woefully lacking under our rules and procedures. It will not help ameliorate the worry in the mind of the government House leader-and I have been on both sides of the House-if threats are made, as he has made them today, in advance about what is going to be his attitude. I think it is important that we move ahead with this bill.
The minister and the House leader have made it clear that there will be several pieces of legislation-I am not sure whether the number is five or six-under the National Energy Program, and this one has been waiting for a long time. It is a highly technical bill which requires expert witnesses to come before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works in order to deal with its technical aspects.
Opposition members such as the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) have asked that the national energy package be put before a committee so that we can get on with the calling of witnesses, people from the industry and people from government departments, to look at the various aspects of the bill. By moving this bill into committee now we will have an opportunity to do that.
It seems to me that this bill is related to a great extent to the supply of energy and to providing a firm basis upon which oil exploration and development can take place in the Arctic and off the east coast. We now hear that there is more interest in the west coast offshore as well, so it is important that we get on with this bill at this time.
There are other aspects of the National Energy Program to which this bill is related, and those aspects are also important. It is important that this bill deals with the Canadianization of the industry. This bill would allow the federal government to have a 25 per cent carried interest in oil and gas exploration and discovery on Canada lands. The bill requires a 50 per cent Canadian ownership.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) talked about a wrong-headed policy. The national energy policy provides for reasonable and moderate increases in the price of energy during the first four or five years of the policy and then a more rapid escalation during the last five years of this decade, at the same time providing incentives so that consumers will moderate their use of oil through conservation and substitution. There will be bills coming before this House during this session of Parliament relating to conservation and conversion from oil and gas. All these bills must be dealt with. It seems to me that if we spend more than what will be about five days on just one bill at the second reading stage, we will never get to dealing with the several other bills which are also important to the implementation of this policy.

Mr. Speaker, I have been asked a number of times how I felt about coming to Parliament and acting as an MP, and I can tell you that one of the very unpleasant experiences I have had here is to listen to members, such as the one who has just spoken, twist the truth and make misleading statements which border on the untruth and which are misleading to the people who are listening to them. He knows this, and he should not waste the time of the House by poisoning the atmosphere and by poisoning the minds of the people who are listening to this debate. That is the sort of thing that ruins Parliament, the sort of thing that makes the people of this country lack in respect for members of the House.
A little over a year ago our government invoked Standing Order 75c, and at that time a member opposite made the following statement:
Mr. Speaker, this is indeed a sad day for Parliament and democracy when we are faced with the irresponsible and ill-advised actions of this government. They want to rule Parliament by force, they resort to every possible and conceivable trick to prevent the people's elected representatives from expressing their views and those of their constituents and putting forward sensible alternatives to this government's proposals.
The debate was on our bill for mortgage deductibility, a debate which had lasted seven days. Now the same Standing Order is invoked in this Parliament after only three and a half days' debate on a bill, and I have yet to hear any arguments such as those expressed by that Liberal member about a year ago. At that time the Liberals were screaming that we were gagging and stifling Parliament. We have not heard anything like that this time.
1 was very upset to hear the tone of the statement by the House leader who threatened that if we do not toe the line of the government, we will have more of rule 75c, not less. That is a very sad thing for Parliament after we have had rule 75c on borrowing authority, and closure on the constitution proposal. It is ironic when you think that here is a government, which is spending a great amount of parliamentary time and effort in moving toward a bill of rights which will entrench a charter of rights and which will protect the rights of people in this country, walking over the rights of members of the House without any concern for the views which are being presented and the views of constituents whom members of the House represent.
One of the benefits of debates in this House, apart from the fact that some very good ideas are put forward here, is that members opposite are forced to listen to arguments and views which might not agree with those which are being presented by their government to their caucus. It is an educational process, and it pleases me to see some hon. members listening attentively to the very good speeches which are being made on this side of the House on the very important pieces of legislation brought forward, particularly on the matter of energy.
There is a very important logic behind the rules of the House, which is that the rules enforce upon the House the discipline of listening to the various points of view presented on something as complex and technical as is Bill C-48 which will affect the development of Canada lands for years and generations to come. It is impossible to do justice to this proposed legislation in just three and a half or four days. As the opposition leader has just pointed out, we were not stretching out the debate when the government House leader served notice that he would introduce Standing Order 75C. He was the tenth speaker. We had only nine in this party, and three speakers had spoken for the NDP.
You have to ask yourself: when we have the duty to examine this important legislation being brought forward by the government, what is the government hiding behind, why is it invoking closure at this time of the debate, why is it hiding behind the argument about the impact that this will have on supply? The impact will be devastating, as is starting to come out during the NEB hearings on supply which have been rescheduled and updated because of the impact which the NEB knows the National Energy Program will have on supply in this country.
Why is the government hiding behind the argument of the impact on Canadianization? Canadianization, or the policy which is set forward by the National Energy Program, is going to hurt companies the most, the ones which it was designed to help. To me that is absolute nonsense. Canadianization, as members on all sides of the House agree, is a good thing for the country, yet the bureaucrats and the minister on the other side do not have the intelligence to come up with a set of proposals in a policy which would allow Canadianization to take place.
Over the past years we have seen a very healthy increase in Canadian ownership in this industry. That process had continued until October 28 and it was on that date that it stopped. The unfortunate part of this whole policy, in our view, is that Canadian ownership will not increase in the ordinary way through private enterprise, through independent Canadian-owned companies. It will only increase if the federal government, through PetroCan or some other state-owned company, will be forced to take over companies and increase state ownership of the industry. This will not happen in the ordinary course of events.
Why is the government hiding behind the argument about the impact of this policy on jobs in Ontario and Quebec and on investor confidence in this country? These are the important issues which we have been trying to bring out in this debate,
January 13, 1981

and which we will continue to do respecting the future elements of the energy policy. It is important that the people in the country understand them and do not allow the government to hide behind motherhood statements on Canadian ownership, when Canadian ownership will suffer, and motherhood statements on security, when supply will go down in this country. These are the things that we as the responsible opposition must bring to the attention of the people of Canada.
Let me point out that there are some very good speakers who have not spoken in this debate. At the time the government House leader rose in his place yesterday, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) were in the course of very important speeches on the impact of the international energy climate on energy in this country. In the case of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, we received the very great benefit of his long experience as a member of the House of Commons, and all also as a former minister who had worked hard and lived with the problems of devising regulations for the development of our north.
We have yet to hear from the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who will discuss the impact of this program on offshore resource ownership and on the people of the provinces of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. We have yet to hear from the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) who has studied very carefully the impact of the energy program as it relates to increased discretion by ministers, increased government regulation, and what this is expected to do in the development of our resources.
This bill is of critical importance to the development of our energy resources not for the 1980s but for the 1990s and the future. If the development does not take place at a proper pace and with a proper set of rules, we will waste valuable energy in this country which we will never see again. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said last night, we will be high-grading the resources of the country to the detriment of our children, our grandchildren and their children. That is why we feel we must draw out the very important elements of this policy.
If the government persists in the overbearing and arrogant attitude that "we have heard enough; let's get on with the next job; we will not listen to any more of these arguments with which we feel uncomfortable", then this government, this Parliament, and Canada will suffer seriously. The threat of Standing Order 75c being used more in the future does not bode well for Parliament. We will have a very rough time as we carry through on what we hope will be a good energy policy. But, it must be changed and completely rewritten if it is to serve the purposes of this country. That is why we feel it is important that this debate continue on and why we will be voting against the motion in the vote later today.
