Mr. Speaker, this motion by the government to close off debate is despicable and outrageous. It is all of those adjectives which could and should be used to describe it. But, perhaps more than that, it is tragic in a real sense that more than just this bill is involved, more than just this vitally important national energy policy is involved. It is really one more nail, if you will, one more bit of pressure on what little parliamentary democracy we have left.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had some valuable suggestions to make, in terms of trying to find some resolution to this perpetual problem of time exigencies or desires of the government and the needs and desires of Parliament. I thought-and, granted, there may not be time now to discuss it-perhaps he might have looked more deeply at the threat this type of action poses, yes, to our very democracy.
I am not a scholar of history but I am aware of some of the history of our Canadian parliamentary system and parliamentary democracy in general. There was a time not too many years ago when the executive, seeking to have a bill passed by a legislature, was required to convince that legislature of its merits. It was required to present argument, lobby, twist arms and do those kinds of things, since members sit as full-fledged representatives of their constituents, and are free to vote based on their best judgment, based on what the needs of the nation and their constituents are. The growth of parties put that to an end. It is directly attributable to the existence of executive power.
Clearly to the Prime Minister and his cabinet it is not particularly satisfying to go around and convince people of the merits of their legislation. It is much easier to be able to announce it and count on undivided, unquestioning and uncritical support. They could get that by use of the Prime Minister's ability to appoint, to promote to the cabinet or as parliamentary secretaries those who are most loyal, and most willing to punish, by sending them to the back rows, those who perhaps object or think on their own. Through that facility, successive prime ministers, not of any particular party, were able to count on the undivided support of each and every one of their members. Therefore, once an election was over they no longer needed to worry about convincing anybody about the
January 13, 1981

merits of a piece of legislation or motion put before this House.
But Parliament was still not totally without power. Parliament had the traditional ability to hold up supply until grievances were answered. It was a large power which enabled this body to hold ministers accountable in a real way. But some changes in the rules, I believe in 1964 or 1965, did away effectively with that power of Parliament, leaving members of this House with only one power-the ability to make a speech in this House, have it reported to the public, thereby hopefully affecting public opinion. That then might hopefully influence the government to alter its course or take into account the arguments presented. That is a very minor, almost insignificant power, considering the responsibilities which are supposedly vested in one who seeks election and is elected by his fellow citizens to represent them here in the national government.
Now we have this government moving against that very insignificant power which is left to members of Parliament. Even that insignificant power is too much in the mind of this government. As the government House leader indicated today, it is his intention to use 75C frequently to ensure that we do not speak too long, and to ensure that the message being presented here does not get around to the people in the countryside so that they have a chance to think about it and bring back their feelings and opinions.
Mr. Speaker, in all sincerity I ask do you still have a democracy if all that is left is once every few years, at a time chosen by the government-obviously it will choose the most opportune time-you have an election, whilst in between there is nothing else? If those of us who are elected, and we are not elected to support the majority party, are not some of the chosen few to sit on the treasury benches, if we have no say in the legislative process of this country; if we have no say in the governing of this country, and if we should not debate in this House since that might influence public opinion, I ask you is that a democracy?
When you add to that the ability and the demonstrated willingness of this government to utilize polling and advertising to mould public opinion I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what is left? I ask members opposite to think about that for a while and, when they look at themselves in the mirror, to say, why was I elected? Was it to say "Aye, sir, aye" whenever the government asks me to? I ask you to ask yourselves why you were elected, and to ask if your responsibilities do not go deeper than that.
While 1 am in the mood I might do a little media bashing. It certainly disturbs me to see how the media of this country will go into a froth and rage when someone dares to cut out a pornographic scene in a movie. That is treading on freedom of the press. That is anti-democracy and it is terrible. But let the government tromp on the privileges of members of Parliament and they say, "What are you talking about? They are just members of Parliament. What do they amount to in the scheme of things? What is important is that they should not cut any pornography out of movies, that is what is important.
Public Bills
That is one small step and who knows what it will lead to in terms of tromping on the press?"
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised in a peripheral way some very important questions about this second reading debate and about the operations of the House and its rules. I suggest that the time has come when we should be looking at the fundamental rules of this House and the way in which we operate in order to determine if we are any longer a parliamentary democracy in the real sense of the word. speechtext:
that Bill C-223, respecting representation in the Canadian House of Commons, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. I do not intend to use the maximum time allotted to me because I would like to hear from members opposite the government's intentions with regard to redistribution in the future. The purpose of Bill C-223 is to maintain the membership in the House of Commons at approximately the present level until the population of Canada exceeds 50 million.
My thesis is that we should keep the total membership in the House of Commons at 282 members. We should keep the total number at a manageable level, and 282 seems to me to be the optimum figure. I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and perhaps others in the House, would like to see the figure cut back somewhat in order that members may become more effective. I question whether such a move would be acceptable to the House of Commons. However, I trust that the government will seriously look at the possibility of maintaining the membership in the House at its present level.
I do not feel that there is the demand or the necessity to increase the total membership of this House after each decennial census. The House of Commons is cumbersome and unwieldy enough as it is presently constituted. At present Parliament is a $100 million per year industry in Ottawa. There are 282 members of Parliament, 104 senators, and more than 3,200 personnel on the support staff. That works out to about $250,000 for every member of Parliament and senator, which is all paid for by the taxpayers of Canada.
Maintaining the membership at the present level would cut down on costs and ensure that individual members do not become lost in the crowd. I for one feel that members of Parliament and their constituents would suffer in the long run if the membership were increased because members of Parliament would be less effective and the power of the Prime Minister and the executive arm of the government would become more powerful. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in my opinion has too much authority now.
Recently, the minister responsible for Statistics Canada said that after the 1981 decennial census he expects that 30 new federal seats will be created and that the majority will be west of the Ontario-Manitoba border. On the basis of present figures and projections which I obtained from Statistics Canada, I question his arithmetic in that he only projects five new electoral districts for Alberta. His prognostications and the figures from Statistics Canada just do not meet up. He said that on the basis of a projected population growth of 14.9 per cent in Alberta from 1976 to 1981, Alberta would get five new seats. British Columbia should have the second largest population increase in 1981, a projection of a 7.4 per cent increase from 1976 to 2.6 million. Manitoba and Saskatchewan will presumably have much lower growth rate percentages.
Using the projection of 14.9 per cent growth for Alberta for five seats, how can these projections add up to 15 more seats for western Canada? Simple arithmetic tells me that we will be lucky if we receive a third of the 30 new seats under the minister's plan, if he or the government decides that they will go ahead with the plan. Canada's approach is supposedly representation by population.
In practice, the system is not working fairly and the provincial numbers are out of whack. How it works is that as a result of the 1974 BN A Act amendments, after each decennial census, or ten-year census, the seats in the Commons are redistributed. Quebec's population is used as the base figure in
January 13, 1981

this redistribution. After each census, regardless of the population increase, Quebec automatically receives four new seats in the Commons. The number of Quebec seats is then divided into the total number of population in Quebec, and this provides a barometer for the number of constituents which will be represented by a member of Parliament. The seats are then redistributed across Canada on the basis of this figure which should be in the vicinity of 80,000 people. The problem is that by the time redistribution is implemented, the figures are stale by three or four years or, as after the last census in 1971, outdated by eight years.
This year we will have a decennial census. The final figures will not be available until 1982 or perhaps, at the earliest, in late 1981. This means that we might have royal assent to amending legislation in 1983 or 1984, or 1988 or 1989, as happened last time. Nevertheless, redistribution will be implemented using stale and outdated statistics.
A member of Parliament from Quebec presently represents approximately 83,000 people; an MP from Manitoba, 87,000; an MP from B.C., 90,000, and an MP from Alberta, 93,000 people.
With present trends continuing, by 1983, the earliest redistribution can take place, it is anticipated that the average population of electoral districts in Alberta will be in the vicinity of 105,000 people, approximately 20,000 over the national average.
Automatically increasing the size of this House every ten years hardly qualifies as reform. If we are to effect parliamentary reform we must take a long and searching look at the optimum size of this chamber.
The United States, with ten times our population, is able to conduct the nation's business with a fixed Congress of 465 congressmen and 100 senators. In the United Kingdom there are 635 members of Parliament for 60 million people.
I scarcely feel that the quality of Parliament or its workings will be improved by adding to its numbers. We should first seek to improve Parliament, to streamline it, to make it more effective.
May I suggest that we first of all examine the committee system. Most committees are mere window dressing for the government. Most committee members are given the mushroom treatment. They are kept in the dark and, every now and then, the government opens the door and throws a load of you know what on them. Some committees have done excellent work and have produced excellent results, but these are few and far between. The average standing or select committee has far too little time and far too little support staff to be effective.
Further, if we are serious about reform we should look to the Senate. The Senate, with its wealth of talent and experience, is badly underutilized. It should be a more effective and more useful appendage of Parliament. The Senate represents the compromise which enabled the four original provinces to combine federalism with the British parliamentary system
Parliamentary Representation
since it was intended to protect the less populous regions such as Quebec and the maritimes by giving them equal representation with Ontario. Later, the west was also given equal representation.
The Senate was designed to be a protector of the interests of the provinces or regions. It was intended to be a revising and restraining body to deal with possible errors or impulses of the Commons. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the Senate will measure up to this responsibility in our present constitutional dilemma. It was to be a chamber of sober second thought and a counterbalance to the popularly elected chamber.
Lastly, the Senate was to represent property and conservatism. The interests of private property were always in a minority in a democratic society and the Senate was expected to protect those rights.
The Senate once enjoyed more political influence than today. In the first Canadian cabinet, five of the 13 ministers were senators, and two governments in the nineteenth century were led by senators. Practically every major portfolio, except finance, has been held at one time or another by a senator.
The Senate frequently confronts the impossible task of giving adequate consideration to important bills which are dumped on it shortly before the end of a session or just before a recess.
In recent years the Senate has done some extremely useful work in investigations of major social and economic issues through its committee system. Its initiatives in this area have sometimes made the appointing of royal commissions unnecessary.
The Senate can be a very useful partner in Parliament if its terms of reference and its mandate are reviewed, revised, and reformed.
There is some validity to the thesis that senators be elected, so that they are looked upon with more respect and credibility by the Canadian people.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I say, keep the membership in the House of Commons at its present level. Do not dilute the product by indiscriminately adding to our numbers.
Make better use of what we have. Make better use of the committee system in both chambers. Make better use of the joint committees which exist. Examine the Senate with a view to modernizing its functions and its role in a bicameral system of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not use all the time available to me either. I should like to thank the hon. member for bringing this very important and interesting matter, which is more complicated than it appears at first glance, before us for discussion.
The question of representation and the number of members that should be elected is an important one, as is the larger question of proportional representation. It is difficult for the

public to understand the complexities, almost an impossibility, of arriving at a system which will ensure fair representation of all parts of the country in the House of Commons. On the one hand, there is the obvious and undisputable need for representation by population, for reasonably equal number of people to elect a member and, of course, the need in a country as large and underpopulated as ours, for adequate representation. There is evidence of this in the House every day when we discuss issues that affect areas that do not have a large population.
This problem is more acute in Canada than in countries that have a population which is spread evenly across the land. In the eight years that I have been in this House, Mr. Speaker, members from western Canada have often brought to our attention the fact that until recently representation was weighted in favour of eastern and central Canada. There were fewer members from some of the prairie provinces because of the fact that their population was not great. I believe this problem is gradually being corrected in British Columbia at least, which is now termed a heavily weighted province for the purpose of determining the numbers of constituencies to be represented.
I represent what in the United States is termed an inner city constituency. It is in the centre of the city of Toronto. We who represent downtown constituencies face the problem of populations moving to the suburbs. It could be argued that the core areas of the cities are losing representation because of the suburban phenomenon. Ironically, we now face the same problem as members from the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan in that we are losing representation in the city while the outlying areas appear to be gaining representation. I think the most interesting example of that occurs in the United States.
Many of the major cities in the eastern United States, including New York, Philadelphia, Boston and Detroit, are challenging the U.S. census by taking the matter to court. The reason for the challenge, they say, is undercounting. As a result they are losing representation in Congress, which is part of the same problem the hon. member has brought to us for discussion. It is a very complex one.
In a democratic country everyone agrees that similar numbers of people should be electing a representative on their behalf. On the other hand, there are areas where the population is so spread out we find people do not have the same interests. It is not unreasonable to find that people living hundreds of miles apart do not share the same interests and so feel they should have two representatives, or perhaps more. We could easily have one million people sharing one interest and have 2,000 people with another interest. There are still only two interests even though they are off-weighted by population. That problem is far more serious in Canada than it is in Europe and much more serious than in the United States, although people from the Rocky Mountain area in the United
States feel they are under represented because of their small population.
The way in which redistribution is conducted in Canada is a far more complicated process than most members of the House have ever realized. It is a complex business which has changed and is changing, so I will refer to my notes. For nearly all of our history, redistribution was carried out within very fixed bounds. We set the membership of the House at a certain number and worked from that number. One of the problems which became evident in the early 1970s was that it is virtually impossible to protect the representation of the smaller provinces, if we look at it from a provincial angle, while adding members to represent fast-growing population areas.
A surprise to me, which I am sure it will be to other members of the House, is the projected membership of the House of Commons, if predictions are correct. I do not think they will be because those predictions have not been correct so far. According to Statistics Canada population projections, the size of the House of Commons, which is presently 282 members, and before the last redistribution was 265-

Different formulae are always being brought forward, but then someone says that for 100,000 people here a member should be elected and for 100,000 people there a member should be elected. Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery), I believe the subject matter of this bill rather than the bill itself should be referred to an appropriate committee so that that subject matter can be studied. In that sense 1 congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) for bringing the bill before us. 1 liked parts of his speech. He knows there is one section which had nothing to do with the bill which would not get my approval. That is the section where he praised the other place. There are a lot of fine men and women over there, but the institution of a second House that is not responsible to the people of this country in my view is one for which there is no place in a parliamentary democracy. However, the Senate is not part of the bill, so one does not have to deal with it at any great length.
The main concern of the hon. member in introducing his bill, as 1 understand it, is that we not leave ourselves open to a course which will result in this place having 325, 350 or 400 members a few decades down the road. Where we would put them is one problem. Apart from that, there is the problem of the efficient operation of the place.
There is one word of assurance I should like to give the hon. member. I do so out of experience. 1 have been through four redistributions since coming here. The hon. member across the way talked about the 264 members we had a while ago. When I first came here, the membership was only 245. In each ten-year period that we have looked at redistribution, we have changed the rules. One would think that when you write a rule about redistribution, it is the law of the Medes and Persians, that it is going to be there for all time. However, every decade that goes by produces a new set of problems.
Parliamentary Representation
In the late forties and fifties, we had a problem in the prairie provinces in that we were losing members. When I came here in 1972, we had 17 members from Manitoba and that number or more from Saskatchewan. Those provinces have not lost population. They have more population today than they had then. It is relativity which comes into the picture. It is the larger populations of Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and Alberta which left those provinces in that position.
We had a very interesting cabinet minister from Saskatchewan named Jimmy Gardiner. He did not like to see Saskatchewan go down so fast. In one of the redistributions when he was in a powerful position, he persuaded the government to bring in the Gardiner formula which said that no province could ever lose a number of seats that was more than a certain percentage of the total that it had. For ten or 20 years we followed that rule. It protected Saskatchewan and Manitoba and, at one point, Nova Scotia. However, the day came when that rule did not seem to be meeting the needs and we changed it again.
Away back, as we all learned in school, the House was composed of 65 members from Quebec and the numbers from the rest of the provinces were in proportion thereto. In Mr. St. Laurent's time, we changed all that. We decided on a total number of members to be divided according to certain rules of proportion. Indeed, the last time we came back to a fixed number from Quebec. This time, however, it was fixed for one time at 75 and it is to go up by four every decade.
The point I am making is that every time there is a redistribution, an immediate problem comes along. We had to save the prairie provinces, we had to save Nova Scotia or something like that, so we devise a rule which fits what we wanted to do. I think I can say quite straightforwardly that when the present system was put in, it was said it would get us over the hump, that we are not really going to go on increasing the number in this House far past the 300 mark.
I believe it is a foregone conclusion that there will be a consideration of the whole matter. It would be a good idea to start that consideration now. That is why I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) that this bill not be talked out, but that the subject matter of it be referred to the appropriate committee.
At the same time, we better look at a few other things. These are all pretty closely related to the constitutional discussions now going on. We have to look at the whole question of an assembly which is a mixture of members who represent constituencies and members on the basis of proportional representation.
This subject has been discussed by the academics from A to Z. There are those very strongly in favour of it and those who are very much against it. I do not think in this country we could go for complete proportional representation. There are now 14 of us from Manitoba. If Manitoba were on a PR basis, and if I were one of the 14 members from Manitoba, it would be much more difficult to feel one was a member in that way than for each of us to be a member for a constituency.

1 contend that a mixture of members directly representative of constituencies and proportional representation would be useful to consider. One reason is that it might solve the problem of having so many parliaments in which some provinces are represented by only one party. We have that situation right now. I do not know whether the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) has resigned yet or not, but if and when he does, the province of Quebec will have only Liberals. Alberta has only Conservative members in the House of Commons. There are some Liberal supporters in Alberta, Conservative supporters in Quebec and NDP supporters all over the country.

Mr. Speaker, while I welcome the opportunity to speak on this subject, I have on the order paper somewhere a motion to deal with redistribution and the method by which it is done. It is a peripherally related matter.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated, a number of points have been put forward by members with regard to representation and how we choose this House. They should go into the hopper now, not on the eve of the next election. It should not be as we did in 1974 after a redistribution. We saw a cat's breakfast served up by the redistribution commission in their wisdom. As my former colleague from Carleton said, never was there such gerrymandering, incompetence and ignorance as was exhibited by the reports generally during that redistribution. That was incompetence and ignorance as far as political representation was concerned.
In so far as this House is concerned, I am going to take another tack. 1 thought it was deplorable that in 1974 in order to again emulate the philosophy of the late Jimmy Gardiner, certain interests had to be placated. The census was in 1971 and it was about 1973 that we got the commissioner's reports. Saskatchewan was being run right down because the population had dropped, Manitoba even more. Horror of horrors, Quebec was going to lose a seat.
[ Translation]
That was unheard of, unthinkable.

Therefore, a new formula was devised, the one we have at the present time. Earlier I was shaking my head in sheer wonderment at this business of the House escalating within a matter of 15 years to 340 members. It was increasing in greater proportion than the population of Canada and so we arrived at a quotient. This quotient was then reapplied to the member some 23 years ago, there was a floor, a senatorial floor, and the formula for devising the number of seats took the populations of those provinces which were at a senatorial floor out of the general total, and then one divided the then number of remaining seats into the remaining population and arrived at a quotient. This quotient was then reapplied to the populations of the provinces, and we got the number of seats for those provinces. That is how we arrived at 264, and I think it was 265 for the proposed redistribution in 1973-74. I think the hon. member from Cape Breton was the author, or at least he was the sponsor of the plan we have now under which we go by mathematical progressions upwards. No one has yet invented columns made of rubber so that we can instal seats at the far end of the chamber. For you, Mr. Speaker, I think we will have to build a recess and put Your Honour under the gallery because we will require more seats to move up to 312.
This will be fun. Perhaps we will have some balconies. That is another way of doing it. We will have loges off the galleries for hon. members. They shall be those proportionally elected members about whom the hon. member speaks. They will be up there floating, not having had to fight in constituencies. They will be a class apart.

Some of my hon. colleagues may recoil in horror at my own view, which is not, as my colleague suggests, that the present membership of this House be fixed at 282 but that we apply a 20 per cent cut to the representation or by some 56, down to 225.
I can take hon. members through all the sinuosities of the committee system and in this House. Instead of having 30 or 40 people scrambling to get on speaker's lists, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette) would be in his seventh heaven; he would not have to protest about too many people wanting to speak. In fact, some government backbenchers might be able to speak. It
January 13, 1981

would be known as the emancipation formula since at present they are now gagged during a second reading debate. In committee, instead of having 20 people trying to get their ten minutes, there would be only perhaps 12. Some work would be done in committee, and committees could be reduced in size. One might ask, "At what cost?" Well, I remember that there were about 135,000 to 150,000 people in my riding before the first redistribution in 1968. With less staff than I have now I looked after my constituency quite well, I thought, and so did other people. True enough, our work is now more involved. We did not have constituency offices then, but with properly trained legislative assistants or office administrators whom members do not have at the present time, and in the light of improved communications, travel and equipment which is available, members could more than adequately serve double the populations they serve now, and perhaps even better.
It is true enough that some adjustments would have to be made for some of the rural areas. We would have to pay some attention to the historical entitlements of the Atlantic provinces, but a 20 per cent cut does not disturb as much as increasing the size of this House, and in that regard, since we do not want Saskatchewan to lose any more members we will merely increase the size of the pond in which they have to swim; one would drown them just as easily that way; we will just add more water to the bath. The effort was totally cosmetic.
I think we should look at all these suggestions. I know there will be some difficulties with respect to my ideas, but I think this House would function eminently more successfully if there were only about 225 members. After all, the U.S. Senate functions very well, and some senators represent ten million or more people. Two senators from California represent the number of people there are in Canada. They have large adequate staffs. Actually, it costs less to staff their offices properly and to provide them with the appropriate organizations to service their people than it costs us. Being on the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services I can tell hon. members that there is now getting to be a very substantial expense to support each member.
Adding just one member means not just one salary but also all the attendant expenses which go with a member. Representation becomes extraordinarily expensive but, 1 suggest, not any better. Somebody at one of the Toronto newspapers today must have had his tongue in all the cheeks he possesses, both up and down, because he suggested that this House should have 800 members. He just had to be spoofing.
Without wanting to repeat myself again, I must say that I think it is an excellent idea to examine this bill. I trust there will be someone from the government side who will move to amend the motion which is on the order paper. We in the opposition certainly consent fully to withdrawing the bill and the subject matter going to the appropriate committee for consideration and report. I presume that committee will be the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. 1 would be quite prepared to second such a motion. It is my understanding that the parliamentary secretary to the government House
Parliamentary Representation
leader would be prepared to move such a motion, so I am quite pleased to yield the floor to him in the hope that that will be done. There may be others who may wish to participate, but I certainly hope this bill is not talked out and that, as agreed, the subject matter will go forward to the appropriate committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see this bill before the House this afternoon because 1 think this is an important matter which needs to be dealt with in a standing committee of this House. I believe the 1974 Representation Act requires that the President of the Privy Council refer the whole question of representation to a standing committee.
Section 7 of the act suggests that this be done after the House meets. Of course, we have had an interim period of another Parliament in between, during which the whole question of representation was supposed to be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
1 find the suggestion of the hon. member that the whole question be investigated to be very worth while. A few days ago I received a projection from the chief electoral office of the number of seats there will be in the House after the next redistribution in 1981. The projection shows some 30 more seats. Of course, the ridings are divided up only on the basis of projections at this stage, but it seems to me we will end up with a much larger House, not necessarily with better arrangements.
The one matter I think should be considered by the committee, and in fact there is a reference to that committee now, is the question of the large rural ridings. This whole question, of course, will be studied by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections because Bill C-211 has been referred to it already. The bill refers specifically to northern Ontario, but there are areas in northern Manitoba, northern Alberta, Saskatchewan, northwest Quebec and, I believe, Labrador which face similar problems, although not identical to those in northern Ontario. The problem is that these are vast areas which are growing ever larger because of increased population requirements, and 1 think there is a need for consideration of a floor arrangement for representation of those vast northern areas in a number of constituencies.
1 certainly see the proposal for this bill going to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for study to be a very worth while one. I believe the Privy Council has the responsibility of referring the whole matter to the standing committee in any event because of the 1974 Representation Act which provides for reference of the matter of representation to a committee. I hope the government will see fit to move a motion this afternoon to refer this private member's bill, to the standing committee as I think it deserves serious investigation and study as proposed by the hon. member this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a few remarks on Bill C-223 which is now before the

January 13, 1981
Parliamentary Representation
House. Let me begin by congratulating the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) for bringing this matter to the attention of the House because, like other hon. members, 1 agree it is important to consider the matter of the number of people who represent various constituencies and parts of this nation in the House. However, there are other matters to be said with respect to representation of the people of Canada in this House. While I agree that the matter should be studied, some of these other matters might be brought to the attention of members and of the public generally. First of all, we have often spoken of the subject of proportional representation. I draw to the attention of members that without proportional representation of some kind you will get the anomaly of the Progressive Conservative Party, for example, requiring 373,000 votes in the province of Quebec and having only one elected member from there, while at the same time the 357,000 persons who voted for the PC Party in Manitoba and Saskatchewan elected 12 Conservative members from there. So there is an argument for proportional representation. I am not saying I agree with that argument, but that is the kind of thing that might be discussed.
Also, there is quite the contrary view which is presented in an article printed in the Regina Leader-Post in which the writer, Edward Carrigan, writes that he believes the number of members in the House should be increased to 800. He based that concept on the basic representation which prevailed in 1867 and said that at that time the population of Canada was slightly over three million, and has now increased to 24 million. If you make a projection on the basis of these figures, you get a much larger representation. He also refers to the number and complexity of subjects with which the House of Commons deals today and the amount of money expended by the government.
Playing devil's advocate for a moment I wanted to introduce those points because perhaps they are more vital to representation from provinces like Nova Scotia and other provinces in the Atlantic region which might suffer from a move toward representation based entirely on population. I agree to limiting the number of persons who represent people of Canada and constituencies, but I think we should be mindful of the smaller provinces which require basic representation. At present under the BNA Act and relevant legislation, minimum representation is fixed in relation to the number of persons who are permitted to be appointed to the Senate. I think in the case of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, these provinces have now reached the lower limit and their representation in the House is based on the minimum requirements. In the case of Nova Scotia, the province has one more member here than its Senate representation of ten.
We have to be mindful of these considerations when we deal with matters of this kind. I do not want to borrow any phrases from the government side of the House, but let me say that what is at stake here is the quality of representation in the House. As has been said, what Canadians want is effective government, not more government. So the real responsibility is
to make members of Parliament more effective and we can do that with the numbers we have at present.
I will conclude now, Mr. Speaker, to allow a member on the government side to move the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I recognize that I have just two minutes left. Prior to five o'clock 1 attempted to make the point that members of Parliament over the years have had our powers, our ability to represent our constituents, and our ability to act as legislators, removed from us step by step until the point today where we are essentially powerless. We lack even the ability to influence public opinion through giving speeches in the House which are reported, hopefully read and thought about by some people so as to influence their opinion. Let there be no mistake. That is exactly the reason Standing Order 75c was brought in in this case, just as in the case of the constitution when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) originally said, "Look, after all, all we are doing is patriating the constitution at long.last, bringing in a charter of rights and a flexible amending formula. How could one be opposed to that? No one could be opposed to that kind of motherhood thing." Some who did not think of or read what the Prime Minister proposed gave their approval very quickly. It was only after extensive debate and discussion the public realized that was not what was being proposed-much more was being proposed.
Similarly in this case of the national energy policy, Bill C-48, the propaganda says, "Look, what we are doing is Canadianizing the oil industry and trying to make us self-suffi-
S.O.	75c
cient by 1990. How can one be opposed to that?" No one is opposed to that. Those are goals which we and every Canadian accept as reasonable and proper, but anyone looking at the national energy policy, reading it and trying to understand it will recognize that in fact the national energy policy as proposed in its details by the government works in exactly the opposite direction. If, heaven forbid, this policy is implemented, there is not a prayer in the world of this country becoming self-sufficient. We will be on rationing and allocation; that is what will happen. This policy is driving Canadian independent oil companies out of the country.
A couple of members opposite talked about the multinational companies. What they do not seem to recognize is the fundamental fact that the multinationals have nowhere to go. Exxon will not let Imperial Oil go and drill in the United States, nor will Gulf let Gulf Canada do that, nor will Shell let Shell Canada do that. They are stuck here in Canada.

If I were a Tory, 1 would not like it. I can well understand why they do not like the idea of a time limitation. This is why they are on the opposition side, this is why they are Tories. We happened to propose these ideas and we like them. Where it becomes difficult is understanding the opposition, especially on the part of the New Democratic Party. Do they oppose any of these ideas? Perhaps we might hear from them. All we have heard from them this afternoon was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) saying that perhaps we should have an idealistic system whereby we should have a timetable for all the bills at the beginning of a session, without really knowing the implication, the weight and the controversies each bill might have down the road, two or three or four months hence. I ask you how you can do that. It sounds like a very neat, fine theoretical idea but this is not the place for fine, theoretical ideas. At the beginning of a session you decide which bills you should debate and which bills you should not debate. You cannot divide the world into three nice little categories. That is not the way this Parliament works and it will never work that way.
What do we conclude from this? We conclude that we have debated this matter for a total of 12 hours and nine minutes. Therefore, it becomes a matter of judgment. It is a matter of judgment because there will be some who will always think that it is not enough. There will be some who think it is adequate and some who think it is too much. This will be the dilemma which this House will face every time we have Standing Order 75c before us. That is what it has been, a dilemma. It will always be a controversial question. Where do you draw the line between democratic debate and time limitation? That is where you must draw the line sometime, somewhere.
It seems to me that while we are debating this matter, and continue to debate it, the OPEC countries might again increase the international price of oil. So what are we really achieving by debating this matter on second reading after 12 hours of debate already? Why do we do this when all of us who are interested have the opportunity to look at the bill in committee? What the Canadian public probably does not know is that once we give second reading to this bill this matter goes to a standing committee for scrutiny, thorough examination and for the calling of witnesses.

What is at stake here is the public interest. This commodity is too valuable and too essential to the Canadian public to leave to the whims of the private sector. Mr. Speaker, we have had three speakers in this debate. Closure is not a question of balance or a question of judgment, as the hon. member for Davenport said. It is an extraordinary measure. 1 will speak of closure first and then I will speak with regard to what we are talking about tonight-time allocation. There have been four instances of closure since 1956. There was the pipeline debate of 1956, the flag debate of 1964, the debate in 1969 over new rules in this House and the debate in 1980 in respect of the constitution. Time allocation has been used eight times since 1971 by the Liberals and once by the Conservatives. Those are extraordinary measures. This is an extraordinary and shocking performance from the government tonight.
I listened to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), who is a man whom until tonight-and I hope 1 can find a little bit of charity after tonight-I admired very much. He appears to be a very mild-mannered and intelligent minister. But beneath that mild manner there is a deep unreasonableness and there is an hysteria with respect to bringing in this measure. As his leader would say "an hysterical attitude". This closure is not necessary. He made the argument that the bill has to be referred to committee. Well, the committee is not ready yet to hear all the witnesses. He made arguments about there being other energy bills. I happen to know the government does not have other energy bills ready. They do not have an agreement with the provinces about that matter which was raised by one of the members here, the matter of grants for conversions and so on. They do not have an agreement and they are not ready with a bill. So that is not the truth. They should not say that in this House. There is not a more important subject to debate than energy. It was said by the minister that this bill is only part of the energy policy. He says we have debated the energy policy, therefore, we do not need to debate this bill. The minister is wrong there because this is different from what we have been debating. We debated the orders under the Petroleum Administration Act. The member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and I made motions in that debate. But in that debate we debated federal-provincial relations; we debated co-operative federalism; and, we debated pricing. Those are the kinds of things we debated.
We have not debated many of the different but important features of this bill. Who does the minister think he is fooling when he says we have debated these matters? There are matters relating directly to this bill which this House will never hear debated in principle because the government brought in time allocation. Such an example is the issue of offshore oil. Who owns the offshore oil, the provinces or the federal government? An hon. member of my party wanted to speak on that topic in this debate. It will be a most important topic to the country over the next ten years, but it will not be fully debated because of closure.
A member of my party intended to speak on the west coast environment. The government does not have any members from the west coast, so a speaker was appointed to tell the government of the problems there. I hate to tell the hon.
S.O.	75 c
member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) to perhaps support the government in this matter but the hon. members opposite do not want our support, they want to cut off the debate. A member of my party intended to talk on the dangers of the environment of British Columbia and the offshore.
Another member was to speak on the concerns of the fishermen about the Hibernia discovery. Another speaker was appointed to speak about the labour problems and Canadian content. We wanted to fix up parts of the bill to make it better, but the government cut off the debate. Is that logic? I wonder if the President of the Privy Council is as reasonable as he pretends. There have been 12 hours of debate on this bill.
As the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) quite properly said in his comments, "It was not time enough". Closure is used only when there is a flagrant abuse of the time of the House. The onus should be on the government when it brings in closure to show that there has been abuse of the time of the House. In this case there has been no flagrant abuse. I have just listed a number of topics which should be debated, and there are a number of others.
It seems to me the way in which this Parliament should operate is the government should propose and the House of Commons depose. But this government wants to propose and depose as well. I say to the ministers and the backbenchers opposite that they are on a very slippery slope which was started by imposing closure on the Alaska pre-built debate, then the constitutional debate and now finally on this bill.
Some people have said it does not matter because they are the government. People who are watching now and who will not be able to watch when the bill goes to committee, are saying, "Well, does it really matter". I say to the people out there, because you cannot talk to the group across the floor in view of that sheer Liberal arrogance, although it might be for their own good, this debate would have petered out later this week or next week. Mr. Speaker, I should like to extend my thanks to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) for these five minutes.
I should like to put my remarks together rather tightly by saying that last night when I spoke in the debate on Bill C-48, 1 pleaded with members of this House not to regard this as an ordinary bill. This is Bill C-48, regarding oil and gas conservation regulations in Canada lands. I tried to point out to the House and I appealed to the government, particularly to the government House leader, to consider that this was not a judges bill or any one of a number of bills in a $50 billion budget, but that this is the future of Canada. The administration and management of our non-renewable resources is the most important function the federal government has because only the federal government has jurisdiction over Canada lands which comprise several times the total area of Canada, including the land at the bottom of the sea.
This discussion we have held in 12 hours has not even touched the vital principles of this bill. The vital principles require honest and sincere reflection that would take weeks to resolve. We do not have weeks so we have to try to compress the discussion.
Let me give an example. Last night I said 75 per cent of the oil and gas discovered in Norl,h America in the last 100 years remains in the ground, mostly because of bad regulations. The horrible blunder that was made in the American states to the

south and the four western provinces of Canada is a sin that should not be repeated in the Canada lands.
This is not a partisan statement, Mr. Speaker. The future of our country is at stake. We have disgraced ourselves in the four western provinces with the type of regulations we adopted. It was so easy to accept the regulations that the Americans brought with them but when I say Americans, I mean the big international oil companies. As a result of those regulations, the Americans ended up with nearly 90 per cent of the ownership of our oil resources in those western provinces. We do not hate them for that, Mr. Speaker. It was the regulations of the provincial governments which made it impossible for small Canadian companies to grow. We front-end loaded those industries so heavily with bonuses, lease fees, permit fees, every way we could; we gouged those oil companies trying to get as much out of them as we could in the very beginning. As a result, only the big companies could carry the load, for the long pay-out.
1 can remember the day when there were 400 Canadian companies in the west. Few survived but thanks to some amendments to the regulations, a few more have grown in the last few years. In the regulations before us now, Mr. Speaker, we are repeating the same mistake that the provinces in western Canada made 50 years ago.
Parliament did not fail in 1957 and 1961. We brought in regulations that were the best in the world. They were not perfect but at least they preserved about 60 per cent of that total wealth for the Canadian people-and I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people. In the regulations finally brought out by the Liberal government in 1976, about the same proportion could be argued. We accepted the mistakes of the past and we tried to correct them.
I appeal to the House, Mr. Speaker, in God's name-in the name of Canada, do not stop us from trying to bring these ideas forward.
I have four amendments that I want to put forward in this debate. It will take several weeks to get through. I think that on behalf of Canada I have a right to make those constructive amendments. That is all I am asking. Put down this closure regulation or take the bill out entirely so as not to disgrace this Parliament.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, we are going back to the debate on Bill C-48, and these are my final remarks in a speech I started last night. Last night 1 was trying to make the point to the House that the regulations before us now are turning back the clock of regulation-making in Canada by 60 years. Under these regulations we are repeating the same mistakes made by the four western provinces in the late 1920s in which billions of barrels of oil were left in the ground. They need not have been left in the ground had we had the proper regulations. These regulations have been before the federal House since 1957 when we wrote off the previous regulations which gave everything to the oil companies in the Canada lands and brought in regulations which were finally made official in 1961. Those 1961 regulations were promulgated after we received the approval of the oil companies both in the petroleum association and in the independent petroleum association. Those regulations received the support of Parliament and were the best effort of any country at that time in trying to bring in regulations that used the principles of conservation to try to get maximum recovery and at the same time to try to give the maximum value of the oil and gas to the people of Canada who own them in trust for future generations. These lands are mostly in the Northwest Territories, the islands of the north, the waters between the islands and the offshore areas as far as we can go across the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic until we meet the nations across the way. That is the international law. As 1 pointed out, these regulations assume that our sovereignty only goes out 200 miles. That is not the international law. There is no mention in it of the 200-mile limit. That is simply a conclusion drawn from the fishing rights and from the convention which is being put through the United Nations at the present time. The current international law gives sovereign rights to the state to develop the bottom of the sea as far as it can go to the nearest nation. The only parts of the world which have boundaries between them are around the North Sea. They were the first nations to realize the importance and the value of the wealth at the bottom of the sea. But we too are beginning to realize it now in Canada. The government comes to the House and tells us that 12 hours is enough in which to debate regulations which do not only involve hundreds of billions of dollars of wealth but which involve a wealth which we will have to measure in hundreds of trillions of dollars. Every part of the world knows that the most unexplored part of the world is in northern Canada-

Order.

The future of Canada depends on these regulations, not the future of some CCF-NDP alliance with the Liberals. All this chatting going on with long lost friends is not the purpose of this debate in the House. 1 am talking about the wealth for the future of this nation which is in greater abundance in these northern and offshore areas than in the land, and yet we vote closure on the debate on a subject such as this when it has not even been debated.
It is not only the Conservative party or the Liberal party that has had to go through this. Last night I mentioned that, after many, many long years of delay and frustration, the Liberal party came out with regulations in 1976 which met nearly all the difficulties not met in this bill. They made a good effort so that the Canadianization of this industry could be made possible. This bill takes away the Canadianization in the Canada lands and drives out Canadian companies. It is just the opposite of what the government's purpose is. Surely a government has the right and duty to listen and should not make that mistake blindly. In 1976 this was recognized by the government, and the official opposition supported those regulations. The regulations of 1961 were just about as good. They were not perfect because no regulations are perfect, but other governments have had the same problem. I am old enough to remember a government coming into power in Saskatchewan where there was not too much oil and gas. It was a CCF government which wanted the oil industry to come to Saskatchewan because the minute that government was elected, the companies stopped their search and moved out. After six years of Gethsemane, trying to make up its mind, here was a government dedicated to the theory of socialism, a government dedicated to the principle of public ownership of our resources, faced with the reality of how to get these resources developed. Would you like to hear now the words of Tommy Douglas who was then the premier, delivered 30 years ago in Saskatchewan? 1 will quote from the official record which reads as follows:
A provincial government has three alternatives with reference to the development of natural resources. The first is that they can alienate all the resources by turning them over to private enterprise.
That is what the federal government did before 1957 to our great resources in the north. He went on to say:
The second alternative which faces a provincial government in the development of natural resources is for the provincial government to develop those resources themselves.
That is blunt enough. It is private enterprise by itself, the government not bothering it, or the government doing it completely. I will read his decision as follows:
The third alternative, Mr. Speaker, is to combine one and two. The third alternative is to say that we will allow private enterprise to come in here and look for minerals, that if they come in we give them security on two points: one, that if they find certain resources, they will be allowed to develop them and, secondly.

that if they set up the machinery for developing them, they will not be expropriated. Those two categorical assurances have been given and I repeat them here, this afternoon.
1 was present in the legislature when that speech was given. 1 knew the Gethsemane that man had to go through, to give up a lifetime to a socialist concept in the face of serving his people the best way he could. He picked the alternative which the Conservative government did in 1957 for the federal lands, the Canada lands. He picked the alternative which the Liberal government did in 1976 after studying the regulations for ten years.
Tonight we are debating a bill which turns the clock back. One does not do it honestly by just handing all the resources to the big international companies, nor by a device which puts in so many front-end loading charges that it takes all the money at once and kills the goose before it lays any eggs. The only companies which can survive that type of thing, as we have found out in Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, are the ones which generate capital from their own reserves or earnings. It would mean the end of all companies that were not worth several billion dollars in reserves. It would mean the driving out of small Canadian companies.
What is the use of standing up in the House and saying that we will Canadianize the north? During the days of war this government turned over the whole north to the Americans for nothing. I remember that. Also 1 remember in 1958 when I sat on the other side saying in the House that they would all be driven out, and they were. We got that territory back; 1 claimed those northern islands and those waters for the people of Canada.

The Americans accepted that claim, and George Ball, their secretary of state, knows they accepted it. Here we are many years later trying to recover the mistakes so that we can manage and develop the oil resources efficiently.
My first recommendation is to throw out this legislation entirely and redraft it. We should go back to the basic fundamental principles of the 1961 and 1976 regulations. If we do not take it out, we have no alternative but to move major amendments of principle, not of detail nor things discussed in committee. The principle is decided on second reading.
I should like to refer to the four principles which I think should be included. First, we must write in statutory form the principle of conservation. This will mean the maximum economic recovery of every field. We must write in statutory form the elimination of all front-end loading charges. No profits should be taken out of the north, no royalties or taxes should be taken out of the north, until the debts are paid off. The enemy of the government, the people and the companies is the same enemy-interest rates. Interest rates not only kill off the little guy, they kill off the big guys as well.
My third principle would eliminate the back-in proposal of 25 per cent which is a breach of contract and put in its place, in statutory form, a contractual agreement which gives the
partners fair and equal treatment variable according to the type of oil and gas they are discovering.
My fourth principle is that Canadian ownership should be a minimum of 50 per cent of all shares of any private company. All shares of public companies should be available on the stock-markets of the world for that part of the subsidiaries which operate on Canada lands, so that Canadians can freely own this country as individuals and not through some government corporation.

I question whether or not that right hon. member had an opportunity to even look at the bill before he made those charges and allegations. Remembering that in fact that kind of charge was made just a few hours ago, I took the opportunity to leaf very, very quickly through the bill in order to see whether it became abundantly clear a person who had a cursory knowledge of the bill, or at least who had perused it, would be able to find anything in the bill which controverted that and made obvious that in fact it was just not true. Canada Oil and Gas Act

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in this debate to speak profoundly against Bill C-48, primarily on environmental grounds. I am happy to see the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Leblanc) in the House tonight. By the time I complete my speech, perhaps on Thursday, 1 hope they will have some idea of the major deficiencies in this bill.
1 should like to deal first with two concerns and to remind hon. members opposite why members on this side of the House are so concerned about the motion that was voted on a few minutes ago.
I would remind hon. members opposite that Bill C-48 was only delivered to members of the opposition 48 hours prior to the debate which began before Christmas. Prior to closure being brought in there was only time for three speakers from this party. 1 would also point out to hon. members opposite that not only does this do damage to the spirit of this place-a place that I have not belonged to for very long and a place that I find to be profoundly discouraging when closure is brought in on matters such as this-but it also damages democratic politics, something that is becoming increasingly fragile throughout the world.
I would remind hon. members opposite of a second point. It is cabinet that directs the production of these documents. Dozens and hundreds of bureaucrats and technocrats work to produce them. The only time available to members of the opposition to make a general overview of the weaknesses and deficiencies of legislation is during second reading. I find it quite confusing, as I am sure most Canadians do, to hear members on that side of the House claim there are abundant
opportunities for issues to be raised in committee. I have sat on enough committees in the year and I have been in this House long enough to know that the general view of a bill cannot be dealt with in committee because there it is considered clause by clause and witnesses are heard.
In my view it is the serious weaknesses and deficiencies of this bill that have caused debate to be closed off, not that the debate on the bill had become repetitive.
I should like to turn now to the question of the environment, Mr. Speaker. Having read the bill carefully and having read the entire "National Energy Program" carefully, 1 can say that Bill C-48 is essentially regressive and reactionary as it concerns the environment. At a time when scientists around the world are demonstrating the need for drastic increases in site specific studies, especially on the marine environment, the minister has proposed a meagre $15 million revolving fund for an area three times the size of the ten provinces of this country combined.
Bill C-48 is the greatest jurisdictional grab of the century that has taken place anywhere in the world, Mr. Speaker.
We are being told this is the greatest Canadianization legislation in the energy field in Canadian history but, in fact, quite the opposite is occurring. What is taking place is the redistribution of Canada's offshore directly into the hands of the minister, the cabinet and the oil industry.
Rather than a careful scientific approach to the environment, which we might have expected, we find a clause outlining a $15 million fund for environmental studies of an area three times the size of the ten provinces combined! All of the power to regulate is given to the cabinet. I have gone over the bill clause by clause and I will advise all members of the House to do the same in order to learn how many clauses put matters in the hands of the governor in council which, of course, is the cabinet.
All the power for inviting environmental studies is at the absolute discretion of the minister. I would advise hon. members to read subsection (6) on page 28 which reads as follows:
The minister may direct payment from the relevant fund of the reasonable costs of such environmental studies of Canada lands as he determines are necessary in order to decide whether or not to authorize exploration or development under this act or any other act of Parliament.
What we have is a very limited fund, if we keep in mind the size of the area that requires pre-exploratory and pre-drilling studies. 1 would remind hon. members of the outcry that came from the scientific community regarding Lancaster Sound.
There is a great need for capital to be available for scientific studies so that we may learn what has to be preserved and how it can be preserved if we are to do anything at all in that area, let alone move large LNGs or enter into exploratory drilling activities.
If we consider the bill clause by clause, we see that a lot of power is given to the minister. He is given extremely discretionary powers. As members to my right have pointed out quite correctly, these powers should not rest solely in the hands of the minister but should lie either with an independent board

or directly with this Parliament. Lots of land will go to the petroleum industry.
This evening or perhaps the next time I have an opportunity to speak, I intend to deal with the jurisdiction that is established in this bill over the marine environment of British Columbia. GARRISON DIVERSION-UNACCEPTABILITY OF PROJECT TO CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
I rise this evening to emphasize some points I raised in the House last November 19 concerning the Garrison River diversion project in North Dakota.
The Garrison River diversion project in North Dakota is quite a large irrigation project. If it is completed, it is designed to irrigate something like 250,000 acres of farmland, to supply water to several communities in North Dakota and to supply recreation for people who reside in North Dakota and for people who travel to North Dakota to take advantage of this recreation. Hon. members may ask why we are concerned about it in Canada. If this project is completed, it will transfer water from the Missouri basin to the Hudson Bay basin. We are concerned over what this transfer of water will do to our fishing industry in Manitoba and the salinity which will result and flow down the Souris River into the Assiniboine River, into the Red River directly then into Lake Winnipeg and on into Hudson Bay. The chief concern is what can happen to Manitoba's fishing industry. If this project is completed, with the transfer of water from the Missouri basin to the Hudson Bay basin, will come foreign species of fish, biota which are not necessarily compatible with the fish and fish diseases we have in Manitoba. There is quite a large freshwater fishing industry in Manitoba. Estimates I have seen indicate there could be as much as a 50 per cent to 60 per cent reduction in
Adjournment Debate
the kind of fish we catch in Manitoba. In addition, with the transfer of water, we will inherit these problems with our fishing industry and they are non-reversible. We can transfer water and if we have salinity problems we have a chance to turn off the water to stop the salinity. But once we transfer water which has foreign species of fish, fish biota and fish diseases, we have those problems forever. In essence, there is really no compromise in terms of the transfer of water.
Tests have been carried out by collecting fish and fish eggs. Some have proved to be satisfactory and some have proved to be not satisfactory. Even though there are ones proved satisfactory through engineering studies, we all know that accidents can happen. Once the water comes containing foreign species of fish, we will have infinite problems. That is the concern 1 have.
Politics affect these situations. Politics are such that there should be some area of compromise. In other words, we can get together and have one position as far as the Americans are concerned and one position as far as the Canadians are concerned and reach a compromise. However, in this case there really is no compromise. If the water comes, we get the problem but in terms of an engineering solution and as far as reaching a compromise at a political level, there is really no compromise. That is why I think it is most urgent this government understands the situation and do all it can to convey that feeling to the United States.
It is clearly a federal responsibility because it is an international concern by crossing international boundaries.
I wish to quote from the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty. Among other things, it says:
-the waters herein defined as boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other.
That was agreed to by a ruling of the International Joint Commission several years ago. Since that time the Garrison project has proceeded. It has proceeded slowly. Parts of it not completed yet will transfer water from the Missouri basin to the Hudson Bay basin. My concern is that every dollar spent on Garrison makes it that much tougher to reverse. We know that as projects get nearer to completion there is impetus on the people funding those projects to see full realization of the project. Every dollar allocated, in my opinion, brings the project closer to completion and closer to the transfer of foreign fish species and diseases into Canada. Last spring there was an omnibus bill in the United States whereby funds were allocated to the Garrison project at the same time money was allocated to the problems they had in connection with the St. Helen's eruption on the west coast of the United States. Therefore funding is available to the Garrison to bring it closer to completion.
1 suggested in the House on November 19 that the federal government show some responsibility and leadership by setting up a committee of members of all parties of the House to travel to Washington at the appropriate time when the con-

January 13, 1981
Adjournment Debate
gressional committees are meeting in order to convey our concerns to the new administration. By having a committee made up of members of all parties in this House, the Americans would know this is a non-partisan issue. In addition, we would let them know in quite strong terms that Canadians are opposed to the completion of those parts of the Garrison which could cause problems in Canada.
1 urge the government tonight to accept in principle what I have asked, namely, sending an all-party delegation of members of this House to the United States at the appropriate time. I might add, in conclusion, that this was done quite successfully in the spring with regard to a fisheries problem we had with the United States at that time. I applaud that kind of initiative and hope the government will see fit to follow up on that this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: GARRISON DIVERSION-UNACCEPTABILITY OF PROJECT TO CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government will ensure that the incoming administration and the new U.S. Congress are made aware of the very serious objections we have to the Garrison diversion project. Officials in Washington have already started to identify new contacts which will be necessary to ensure that our concerns about the project are fully understood and our interests respected. We intend to make it clear to the new U.S. administration under President Reagan, as we have to President Carter's administration, that Canada is opposed to any plan which would involve inter-basin transfer of water carrying with it harmful biota, and that we expect the U.S. to live up to its international obligations under the Boundary Waters Treaty.
The suggestion that a delegation representing all parties in the House go to Washington to emphasize to the U.S. Congress the united position of all Canadian political parties on this issue is one which the government is seriously considering. We appreciate the willingness of members of the House to act in support of the government's efforts and we recognize the value of a joint approach. We think it would be wise, however, to allow the new administration to be established in office before making any formal representations. In the meantime, the deferral of funds associated with those parts of the project which might affect Canada is an encouraging step. If they intend to proceed with some aspect of the project, the U.S. State Department will likely propose consultations, preceded possibly by a technical level meeting, soon after the Reagan administration takes office. At such time we should be in a better position to evaluate the possible effectiveness of an all-party delegation in support of other efforts to ensure that Canada's interests will be protected.

CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-EMBARGO ON GRAIN SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.-INTERVENTIONS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to devote a few minutes this evening to a very important issue which concerns all Canadians, specifically grain farmers in Canada. I refer to the grain embargo initiated by President Carter in January, 1980, as a result of the Russian invasion of
Afghanistan, its effects and what the government intends to do in terms of payments to farmers. There are various opinions as to the effectiveness of that embargo. Personally, I think it is minimal.
That has also shown up, incidentally, in the fact that in the crop year 1979-80, which is when the embargo was on, the United States government actually exported more grain than it had ever exported before. It exported somewhere in the neigh-bouhood of ten million tonnes more than in the previous crop year, so in terms of the amounts of grain leaving the country the embargo as such really had a very minimal effect and, if it had any effect at all, if we were in Russia we probably would see some hogs, cattle or chickens which might have gone hungry, but it certainly did not have any effect on anything else.
The question which must be asked of the present government is what will be the position it will take if we end up with another embargo. That possibility is quite distinct. I believe food will be used more and more throughout the 1980s as a weapon. It may be used as a political weapon, but nevertheless it will be used as a weapon. As the world population increases and as the production of food will not keep up, food will become very important to many countries in the world.
Russia and Poland seem to be sparring with each other over whether Russia should invade Poland and over what kind of sanctions Russia should use on Poland. My contention is that we will see another embargo. If it is not a government embargo, there certainly is every indication the United States longshoremen will embargo all grain moving to Russia. This would have a very dramatic effect on grain prices throughout the whole of the trading world. I think Canada should be giving some consideration at this time to the position we should be taking if that happens. I hope the minister is willing tonight to give us some indication of the thinking which has been done either in the Canadian Wheat Board or the department for which he will be answering this evening. On the specific question of the amount of money which should be paid to western farmers because of the embargo itself, it should be between $72 million and $75 million. That is approximately the drop grain prices took throughout the early part of that embargo period, and obviously there is not any party in this House which would consider it fair and just that the western grain farmer should carry a political decision of that magnitude by himself.
This is why the Conservative party, backed by the Liberal party when it came into power, indicated there would be payments going out to the farmers.
My question is twofold. First, in general terms what position will Canada be taking in terms of another future embargo? If it is not in 1981, surely it will come in the next few years as food becomes more of a political weapon than it has ever been before. Second, in terms of the payments which will be going to farmers, when will they be made? When will the money be paid, and am 1 correct that the amount is in the neighbour-
January 13, 1981

hood of $72 million to $75 million which will be paid to western grain farmers?
