speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of restraints on the export of grain to the Soviet Onion has been raised many times in this House. It is clear that the government has one outstanding commitment in this regard, and that is with respect to the level of compensation to be paid to producers for losses attributable to the policy of export restraints. If an announcement on compensation has not been as prompt as some hon. members would wish, it is because of the many factors involved. For example, it has been pointed out that international wheat prices fell in the mid-1980s, but they picked up shortly thereafter and are now at very high levels. It is not at all clear to what extent the drop could be linked to the U.S.-led restraint policy. Nor is it clear to what degree the Canadian producer has suffered. Over all, Canadian grain exports were up 20 per cent to a record level in the most recent crop year. Senator Argue has just announced the final payments for the 1979-80 crop year which involve a cash flow to western producers of some $730 million, and the senator has indicated he will be revising the 1980-81 initial payment levels to reflect the continued trend in international prices.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, let met point out that the government remains committed to compensation and expects to be able to make an announcement very soon.
With respect to the restraint policy itself, I would draw the hon. member's attention to Senator Argue's speech in Calgary last November in which he announced the resumption of normal grain sales to the U.S.S.R., along with a new export contract for 2.1 million tonnes of grain for delivery this crop year. He pointed out, however, that Canada continues to oppose the Soviet aggression which led to the restraint in the first place. Naturally, with a new administration taking over in Washington, the government will look forward to hearing its views on the future of this policy.
Evidently, this is a difficult policy issue, but I think it is fair to say that the western farmer is not at present in an unduly difficult position and that to the extent that he has lost income, he can expect to be compensated in the near future.

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-JUSTIFICATION FOR CERTAIN DEPARTMENT STORES TO INCREASE FINANCE CHARGES
speechtext:
The issue which I wish to raise tonight, Mr. Speaker, goes back to May 14 when I asked a question of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). Basically, the question was whether he would be prepared to take personal action to protect the consumers of this country against what are certainly gouging usurious rates proposed by retail companies for retail financing charges. Let me restate the problem. It was companies like Hudson's Bay and Sears which proposed, because of the government's high interest rate policy, to jack up their retail
Adjournment Debate
credit charges to roughly 24 per cent or 25 per cent. A newspaper clipping on an announcement by the Hudson's Bay Company indicates that their annual rate would effectively be 26.08 per cent a year. It is interesting to note that that particular company in its formative years had a motto which was "skin 'em alive". I notice that those interest rates seem to apply.
I asked the minister, on the broad announcement that Master Charge and Chargex, the oil companies and many of the major retail stores within this country, were making fairly dramatic increases in their interest rates, whether he would be prepared to have his department investigate and report back to the House on the justification for such usurious rates in their finance charges, and if he was not prepared to do that, whether he would be prepared to ask the heads of those companies to come into his office to express to them his serious concern about their treatment of consumers in this country. The minister's answer was very curious. He said, "It is not my fault. Why don't you ask the Minister of Finance?" On another occasion when he was asked the same question, he said, "Well, if people do not like using credit cards, they have other alternatives, such as not using them at all."
The basic problem is that in many retail endeavours you do not have a serious option to using a retail credit card. For example, to rent a car now, unless you carry $300 to $500 in your pocket, you have to use that credit card. Many people whose incomes do not warrant the use of credit cards are encouraged and pressed by the retail companies to use those cards. They are asked to charge rather than to pay cash, and in fact over a period of time we have seen a dramatic increase in persona] bankruptcies which can be attributed not only to high prices but to the use of credit cards and the very high interest charges on those cards.
My question goes back to May 14, but certainly it applies to last Sunday morning when CBC radio ran an extensive program concerning bankruptcies. It appears to me that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs intends to do nothing to protect the consumers on this issue. From what I gather, his approach to it is that the way to control this easy access to credit and these high finance charges is to increase the number of personal bankruptcies in this country. That certainly seems to be the trend that is appearing. Also it seems that these companies are not the ones that get hurt when personal bankruptcies occur. I have numerous letters on my desk from small businesses and credit unions which have also been pinched by these personal bankruptcies. They can ill afford to lose the amount of money they have lost.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General, on the oil company investigation, the position on the urea-formaldehyde problem and automobile safety problems, has completely failed to fulfil his responsibilities to the consumers of Canada. Certainly I expect simply a continuation of the answer which he gave on May 14, but I thank the House for the opportunity of expressing my serious con-

January 13, 1981
Adjournment Debate
cern and the concerns of those people who brought this question forward.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-JUSTIFICATION FOR CERTAIN DEPARTMENT STORES TO INCREASE FINANCE CHARGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the fundamental reason for high interest rates in Canada has been the actual and expected level of inflation in this country, the nexus in these circumstances being that lenders demand higher rates of return and most borrowers have been able to pay those higher rates of return for funds. The federal government places a high priority on the lowering of inflation and thus interest rates.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-JUSTIFICATION FOR CERTAIN DEPARTMENT STORES TO INCREASE FINANCE CHARGES
speechtext: Elow can you possibly say that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-JUSTIFICATION FOR CERTAIN DEPARTMENT STORES TO INCREASE FINANCE CHARGES
speechtext:
Contrary to the popular belief of the NDP, interest rates are a function of inflation and not the reverse, as I have said many times before-apparently it has not been heard. I believe the monetary policy being pursued by the Bank of Canada contributes in a substantial way to the accomplishment of the objective of reducing inflation and subsequently to the reduction of interest rates. A high level of interest rates in the short run is an unavoidable necessity to reduce inflation and interest rates in the longer run. It is conceivable that the Bank of Canada could lower interest rates somewhat for a short period by increasing the supply of money in circulation, but 1 suggest that policy has a basic flaw. The basic flaw is that by increasing the money supply in the way which perhaps would be suggested by NDP policy would aggravate inflation and indeed result in much higher interest rates than are currently the situation.
The source of the recent pressure on both the foreign exchange value of the Canadian dollar and interest rates has
been the rapid acceleration in short-term rates in the United States. This has led to an outflow of funds from Canada and pressure on both Canadian interest rates and on the exchange value of the dollar. The Bank of Canada has followed a reasonable and balanced policy of taking part of that pressure in higher interest rates and part of that pressure in a reduction of the exchange value of the dollar.
